Introducing the Palmyra-mini family: Powerful, lightweight, and ready to reason!

📅 11 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (410 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the team at WRITER is thrilled to announce the release of three fresh open models in the Palmyra-mini family.
  • Sources indicate that the "thinking" models have been trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, which improves their reasoning abilities.
  • GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the team at WRITER is thrilled to announce the release of three fresh open models in the Palmyra-mini family. These models are designed to be powerful, lightweight, and highly performant for their size (1.5B to 1.7B), making them ideal for a wide range of applications with efficient inference.

Sources indicate that the "thinking" models have been trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, which improves their reasoning abilities. We're excited to see what the community will build with these upcoming models!

GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:.

palmyra-mini-thinking-a-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini: Our non-reasoning improved base model, delivering a score of 52.6% on Big Bench Hard (get-answer)(exact_match), making it a fantastic all-rounder for a wide variety of generative tasks.

Industry observers note that palmyra-mini-thinking-a: This variant is your go-to for complex logical challenges. Trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, it achieves an impressive 82.87% on GSM8K (strict match), demonstrating its powerful reasoning capabilities. It has the highest overall average score on benchmarks relative to other models in the release.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b: Pushing the boundaries of problem-solving, this model scores a solid 92.5% on AMC23. It's a great choice when you need a model that can "think" its way through demanding tasks. This has the highest average benchmark scores in the benchmarks AIME24,AIME25, GPQA, HMMT25, HLE, MMLU_PRO,MATH500, LCB relative to the other models in the release.

Recent findings suggest that we're releasing both pass@1(avg-of-1) and pass@1(avg-of-64) results. Benchmarking methodology (sampling parameters: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95): Pass@1(avg-of-1) scores:.

GSM8K through MBPP: collected using lm_eval framework. AIME24 through HMMT25: collected using lighteval framework.

Pass@1(avg-of-64) scores: collected using nemoskills framework.

Since all the base models are Qwen architecture the inference should be runnable on popular inference frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, TRTLLM, TGI.

Recent findings suggest that for palmyra-thinking-b the base model was https://huggingface.co/nvidia/OpenReasoning-Nemotron-1.5B. We ran RL fine tuning and observed that it's capable of improving performance. While Reinforcement learning improved single-shot accuracy (pass@1), it reduced sampling diversity, leading to a drop in majority@64 performance compared to the SFT base model. This highlights a trade-off between accuracy and diversity, and we believe transparency around these findings will spark further research along mode collapse, small model performance and other areas.

Through this work, we've tried to push the boundaries of what's achievable with small parameter models, and we're excited to see how the community will continue advancing inference efficiency without sacrificing performance quality.

The token factory never sleeps

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job.
  • Industry observers note that agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure.
  • Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that SPONSORED FEATURE: Agentic AI turns inference into a round-the-clock production job. Here's what it takes to keep the tokens flowing in the datacenter you already have.

Industry observers note that agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope.

Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI rapidly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly important. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer.

Recent findings suggest that ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It declared two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS.

Agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively.

According to recent reports, while training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both.

Running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many consumers, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour.

Sources indicate that enterprises are moving ahead quickly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey, published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years.

It has been revealed that enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. That means they need to think harder about maintenance windows, existing management tooling and predictable deployment. And they'll often be retrofitting halls whose racks rarely draw more than 30 kW.

In token factory terms, the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System is the core compute engine. Each system puts eight NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, linked by sixth-generation NVLink. ASUS has designed its equipment to support the constraints above. Its customers can choose between the hybrid and fully liquid-cooled models, and they can opt for partial or full rack configurations by buying multiple trays. This enables them to match their facilities' needs.

Industry observers note that the other difference between model providers and enterprises lies in which numbers they care about. Peak performance is different from sustained performance. The first is a specification sheet number, while the second is what the GPU actually delivers hours into a heavy workload.

Sources indicate that production inference tends to run continuously, especially when it uses agents, as opposed to training, which is a sporadic job. So the sustained figure is the one that buyers pay for. Heat becomes a real issue here because when cooling can't keep up, GPUs throttle their clocks to protect themselves. In a token factory, a throttled GPU is a slower production line.

Recent findings suggest that the more advanced the architecture becomes, the higher the stakes get. NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU has raised them to their highest point, delivering up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference per eight-GPU board, according to NVIDIA's sparse specification. This is screamingly fast, but the increased heat per board means less margin before throttling.

ASUS designed both models to put direct-to-chip liquid cooling on every GPU. Only the 3U unit leaves the CPUs on air cooling. ASUS also notes it puts every configuration through a 168-hour stress test.

Sources indicate that as boards increase their compute density, pushing up the power and heat requirements, planning naturally has to move out of the server room and into the facility. That's the case whether you're talking about an entire NVL72 rack or a stack of eight-GPU servers like the ASUS systems.

Recent findings suggest that there are other things to consider beyond heat. Few datacenters run racks drawing more than 30 kilowatts, indicates the Uptime Institute. Yet a single liquid-cooled tray of the ASUS systems draws up to 23.9 kilowatts, and a full rack of nine has a power budget of about 216 kilowatts.

Floor loading and power distribution matter as much as cooling.

NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU raises the stakes again. The eight-GPU format enables organizations to buy their computing power in more granular steps. That's where the two ASUS systems come into their own. With few enterprises needing a training cluster at NVL72 scale, the advantage is that an HGX box lets them buy AI compute in digestible pieces.

Industry observers note that the ASUS systems also come with a 54V busbar and cable-free board-to-board design. ASUS notes this simplifies assembly and improves reliability.

So that's space, power and heat. But a GPU board won't produce many tokens if the network, storage or operational tooling can't feed it properly. Agent workloads move context and data all the time, so east-west bandwidth and local storage are key to effective utilization. Any fresh equipment should ideally slot straight into the enterprise's existing management and monitoring tooling.

ASUS ships the whole rack, including servers, networking, power and storage, as a single blueprint. ASUS pre-validates this AI Factory reference architecture at rack scale so that organizations can plan for future growth. That includes dedicated management nodes and a management switch.

According to recent reports, inside each tray, ASUS has sized the data paths to keep the GPUs fed. Eight OSFP ports on NVIDIA ConnectX-9 give every GPU 800Gb/s of east-west bandwidth to the rest of the cluster, and an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU adds two 400GbE ports. Within the board, the eight GPUs talk to each other over NVLink at 3,600GB/s, ASUS says. The 2U tray takes up to 4TB of DDR5 system memory and has eight E1.S NVMe bays for fast local data access, while the 3U model offers a choice of U.2 or E1.S drives.

The other problem for enterprises putting AI inference into production is service and maintenance. In a liquid-cooled box, routine fixes can mean draining a coolant loop, which is downtime, and lost token output, that most enterprises can't afford, especially when dealing with non-batch workloads such as inferencing. So ASUS set out to make components quicker to swap.

On the 2U fully liquid-cooled model, ASUS did it with independent, tool-less CPU and GPU sleds, each with its own direct-to-chip cooling. On the 3U hybrid, ASUS says the air-cooled CPU sled cuts maintenance time by up to 50 percent.

Sources indicate that services aren't just about server maintenance. They're also about decreasing the time to value for AI. Most enterprises won't have in-house rack-scale GPU integration skills, which is why pre-validation and design services are so key.

ASUS states its services run from early facility assessment through to operations. Its professional services cover five offerings: infrastructure design, deployment, performance optimization, AI platform development and lifecycle management. For rapid deployment, ASUS uses its own automation platform, the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center (AIDC).

So, with an enterprise token factory judged on how reliably it keeps producing rather than on peak FLOPS, in-house AI deployment teams will be back to focusing on the basics, albeit while dealing with an innovative technology. That means they'll be asking questions about sustained performance, heat and power in existing facilities. They'll be looking at integration at the rack level and with management software, along with service windows and deployment time. ASUS is positioning itself as a partner that can answer those questions with the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, which it's making available this quarter.

Find out more about the liquid-cooled ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System.

According to recent reports, last year, we shared a blogpost on watermarking, explaining what it means to watermark generative AI content, and why it's notable. The need for watermarking has become even more critical as people all over the world have begun to generate and share AI-generated images, video, audio, and text. Images and video have become so realistic that they’re nearly impossible to distinguish from what you’d see captured by a real camera. Addressing this problem is multi-faceted, but there is one, clear, low-hanging fruit 🍇:.

To help out, we at Hugging Face have made visible watermarking trivially easy: Whenever you create a Space like an app or a demo, you can use our in-house app-building library Gradio to display watermarks with a single command.

For images and video, simply add the watermark parameter, like so:.

Watermarks can be specified as filenames, and for images we additionally support open images or even numpy arrays, to work best with how you want to set up your interface. One option I particularly like is QR watermarks, which can be used to get much more information about the content, and can even be matched to the style of your image or video.

In a recent development, you can also add custom visible watermarks for AI-generated text, so that whenever it is copied, the watermark will appear. Like so:.

This automatically adds attribution when consumers copy text from AI responses, further aiding in AI transparency and disclosure for text generation.

Try it all out today, build your own watermark, have fun!

Acknowledgements: Abubakar Abid and Yuvraj Sharma collaborated on this work and blog post.

very cool, good step towards transparency! 🤗.

In a recent development, I encourage the development community to adopt watermarks and a comprehensive policy related to identifying AI-generated images and video. If not, I believe there will be legislation and legal "incentives" enforcing such a policy. We must take initiative instead of waiting to respond to a negative event.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3!
  • Industry observers note that leRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status.
  • Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3! In our previous LeRobotDataset:v2 release, we stored one episode per file, hitting file-system limitations when scaling datasets to millions of episodes. LeRobotDataset:v3 packs multiple episodes in a single file, using relational metadata to retrieve information at the individual episode level from multi-episode files. The new format also natively supports accessing datasets in streaming mode, allowing to process large datasets on the fly.We provide a one-liner util to convert all datasets in the LeRobotDataset format to the new format, and are very excited to share this milestone with the community ahead of our next stable release!

Industry observers note that leRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status. Our dataset format also stores general information regarding the way the data is being collected (metadata), including a textual description of the task being performed, the kind of robot used and measurement details like the frames per second at which both image and robot state streams are sampled. Metadata are useful to index and search across robotics datasets on the Hugging Face Hub!

Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems. The dataset format is designed to be easily extensible and customizable, and already supports openly available datasets from a wide range of embodiments—including manipulator platforms such as the SO-100 arms and ALOHA-2 setup, real-world humanoid data, simulation datasets, and even self-driving car data! You can explore the current datasets contributed by the community using the dataset visualizer! 🔗.

Besides scale, this upcoming release of LeRobotDataset also enables support for a streaming functionality, allowing to process batches of data from large datasets on the fly, without having to download prohibitively large collections of data onto disk. You can access and use any dataset in v3.0 in streaming mode by using the dedicated StreamingLeRobotDataset interface! Streaming datasets is a key milestone towards more accessible robot learning, and we are excited about sharing it with the community 🤗.

lerobot is the end-to-end robotics library developed at Hugging Face, supporting real-world robotics as well as state of the art robot learning algorithms. The library allows to record datasets locally directly on real-world robots, and to store datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. You can read more about the robots we right now support here!

Recent findings suggest that leRobotDataset:v3 is going to be a part of the lerobot library starting from lerobot-v0.4.0, and we are very excited about sharing it early with the community. You can install the latest lerobot-v0.3.x supporting this new dataset format directly from PyPI using:.

Follow the community's progress towards a stable release of the library here 🤗.

Once you have installed a version of lerobot which supports the latest dataset format, you can record a dataset with our signature robot arm, the SO-101, by using teleoperation alongside the following instructions:.

Head to the official documentation to see how to record a dataset for your use case.

Recent findings suggest that A core design choice behind LeRobotDataset is separating the underlying data storage from the user-facing API. This allows for efficient serialization and storage while presenting the data in an intuitive, ready-to-use format. Datasets are organized into three main components:.

Industry observers note that to support datasets with potentially millions of episodes (resulting in hundreds of millions/billions of individual frames), we merge data from different episodes into the same high-level structure. Concretely, this means that any given tabular collection and video will not contain information about one episode only, but a concatenation of the information available in multiple episodes. This keeps the pressure on the file system manageable, both locally and on remote storage providers like Hugging Face. We can then leverage metadata to gather episode-specific information, e.g. the timestamp a given episode starts or ends in a certain video.

Datasets are organized as repositories containing:.

LeRobotDataset:v3.0 will be released with lerobot-v0.4.0, together with the possibility to easily convert any dataset currently hosted on the Hugging Face Hub to the new v3.0 using:.

We are very excited about sharing this new format early with the community! While we develop lerobot-v0.4.0, you can still convert your dataset to the newly updated version by using the latest lerobot-v0.3.x supporting this new dataset format directly from PyPI using:.

Recent findings suggest that note that this is a pre-release, and generally unstable version. You can follow the status of the development of our next stable release here!

The conversion script convert_dataset_v21_to_v30.py aggregates the multiple episodes episode-0000.mp4, episode-0001.mp4, episode-0002.mp4, .../episode-0000.parquet, episode-0001.parquet, episode-0002.parquet, episode-0003.parquet, ... into single files file-0000.mp4/file-0000.parquet, and updates the metadata accordingly, to be able to retrieve episode-specific information from higher-level files.

Every dataset on the Hugging Face Hub containing the three main pillars presented above (Tabular and Visual Data, as well as relational Metadata), and can be accessed with a single line.

Most robot learning algorithms, based on reinforcement learning (RL) or behavioral cloning (BC), tend to operate on a stack of observations and actions. For instance, RL algorithms typically use a history of previous observations o_{t-H_o:t}, and BC algorithms are instead typically trained to regress chunks of multiple actions. To accommodate for the specifics of robot learning training, LeRobotDataset provides a native windowing operation, whereby we can use the seconds before and after any given observation using a delta_timestamps argument.

Conveniently, by using LeRobotDataset with a PyTorch DataLoader one can automatically collate the individual sample dictionaries from the dataset into a single dictionary of batched tensors.

You can also use any dataset in v3.0 format in streaming mode, without the need to download it locally, by using the StreamingLeRobotDataset class.

It has been revealed that leRobotDataset v3.0 is a stepping stone towards scaling up robotics datasets supported in LeRobot. By providing a format to store and access large collections of robot data we are making progress towards democratizing robotics, allowing the community to train on possibly millions of episodes without even downloading the data itself!

You can try the new dataset format by installing the latest lerobot-v0.3.x, and share any feedback on GitHub or on our Discord server! 🤗.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we're thrilled to share that Public AI is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Public AI joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

It has been revealed that this launch makes it easier than ever to access public and sovereign models from institutions like the Swiss AI Initiative and AI Singapore — right from Hugging Face. You can browse Public AI’s org on the Hub at https://huggingface.co/publicai and try trending supported models at https://huggingface.co/models?inference_provider=publicai&sort=trending.

The Public AI Inference Utility is a nonprofit, open-source project. The team builds products and organizes advocacy to support the work of public AI model builders like the Swiss AI Initiative and AI Singapore, among others.

According to recent reports, the Public AI Inference Utility runs on a distributed infrastructure that combines a vLLM-powered backend with a deployment layer designed for resilience across multiple partners. Behind the scenes, inference is handled by servers exposing OpenAI-compatible APIs on vLLM, deployed across clusters donated by national and industry partners. A global load-balancing layer ensures requests are routed efficiently and transparently, regardless of which country’s compute is serving the query.

According to recent reports, free public access is supported by donated GPU time and advertising subsidies, while long-term stability is intended to be anchored by state and institutional contributions. You can learn more about Public AI’s platform and infrastructure at https://platform.publicai.co/.

You can now use the Public AI Inference Utility as an Inference Provider on Hugging Face. We're excited to see what you'll build with this new provider.

Read more about how to use Public AI as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

See the list of supported models here.

It has been revealed that the following example shows how to use Swiss AI's Apertus-70B using Public AI as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Public AI API key if you have one.

Note: this requires using a recent version of huggingface_hub (>= 0.34.6).

Industry observers note that at the time of writing, usage of the Public AI Inference Utility through Hugging Face Inference Providers is free of charge. Pricing and availability may change.

Here is how billing works for other providers on the platform:.

It has been revealed that for direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Public AI API key you're billed on your Public AI account.

Industry observers note that for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Important Note ‼️ PRO consumers get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

It has been revealed that we would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

If you use them via Hugging Face’s routing, you may benefit from credits.

If you use them directly (e.g., via API keys), you’ll pay their rates, not Hugging Face’s.

So yes, some usage is free, but not unlimited, and pricing depends on how you connect.

Democratizing AI Safety with RiskRubric.ai

📅 18 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.
  • It has been revealed that more than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to people how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects.
  • Recent findings suggest that as models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.

It has been revealed that more than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to people how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects. Developers might find a model that perfectly fits their use case, but have no systematic way to evaluate its security posture, privacy implications, or potential failure modes.

Recent findings suggest that as models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting. We're therefore excited to announce RiskRubric.ai, a novel initiative led by Cloud Security Alliance and Noma Security, with contributions by Haize Labs and Harmonic Security, for standardized and transparent risk assessment in the AI model ecosystem.

RiskRubric.ai provides consistent, comparable risk scores across the entire model landscape, by evaluating models across six pillars: transparency, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and reputation.

The platform's approach aligns perfectly with open-source values: rigorous, transparent, and reproducible. Using Noma Security capabilities to automate the effort, each model undergoes:.

According to recent reports, these assessments produce 0-100 scores for each risk pillar, rolling up to clear A-F letter grades. Each evaluation also includes specific vulnerabilities found, recommended mitigations, and suggestions for improvements.

Industry observers note that riskRubric also comes with filters to help developers and organizations make deployment decisions based on what’s important for them. Need a model with strong privacy guarantees for healthcare applications? Filter by privacy scores. Building a customer-facing application requiring consistent outputs? Prioritize reliability ratings.

Evaluating both open and closed models with the exact same standards highlighted some interesting results: many open models actually outperform their closed counterparts in specific risk dimensions (particularly transparency, where open development practices shine).

Risk distribution is polarized – most models are strong, but mid-tier scores show elevated exposure.

According to recent reports, the total risk scores range from 47 to 94, with a median of 81 (on a 100 points). Most models cluster in the “safer” range (54% are A or B level), but a long tail of underperformers drags the average down. That split reveals a polarization: models tend to be either well-protected or in the middle-score range, with fewer in between.

The models concentrated in the 50–67 band (C/D range) are not outright broken, but they do provide only medium to low overall protection. This band represents the most practical area of concern, where security gaps are material enough to warrant prioritization.

What this means: Don’t assume the “average” model is safe. The tail of weak performers is real – and that’s where attackers will focus. Teams can use composite scores to set a minimum threshold (e.g. 75) for procurement or deployment, ensuring outliers don’t slip into production.

Safety risk is the “swing factor” – but it tracks closely with security posture.

The Safety & Societal pillar (e.g. harmful output prevention) reveals the widest variation across models. Importantly, models that invest in security hardening (prompt injection defenses, policy enforcement) almost always score better on safety as well.

In a recent development, what this means: Strengthening core security controls goes beyond preventing jailbreaks, but also directly reduces downstream harms! Safety seems like it is a byproduct of robust security posture.

Guardrails can erode transparency – unless you design for it.

Stricter protections often make models less transparent to end users (e.g. refusals without explanations, hidden boundaries). This can create a trust gap: users may perceive the system as “opaque” even while it’s secure.

What this means: Security shouldn’t come at the cost of trust. To balance both, pair strong safeguards with explanatory refusals, provenance signals, and auditability. This preserves transparency without loosening defenses.

An updating results sheet can be accessed here.

According to recent reports, when risk assessments are public and standardized, the entire community can work together to improve model safety. Developers can see exactly where their models need strengthening, and the community can contribute fixes, patches, and safer fine-tuned variants. This creates a virtuous cycle of transparent improvement that's impossible with closed systems. It also helps the community at large understand what works and does not, safety wise, by studying best models.

If you want to take part in this initiative, you can submit your model for evaluation (or suggest existing models!) to understand their risk profile!

We also welcome all feedback on the assessment methodology and scoring framework.

Industry observers note that really insightful breakdown, Gal, the level of depth and transparency RiskRubric brings is impressive, especially given how fast the open model ecosystem is growing. At Openforge.io we’ve worked with teams navigating healthcare and finance compliance, and the lack of clear security benchmarks for AI models is often a blocker for adoption.

Sources indicate that the six-pillar framework feels like a solid step toward building that missing trust layer. Curious, do you see RiskRubric evolving into something that could be integrated into CI/CD pipelines for real-time scoring during development?

Industry observers note that thanks a lot for the thoughtful comment!Yes, RiskRubric can absolutely be integrated into CI/CD or model approval workflows. Several companies that have adopted RiskRubric already use it that way: models that achieve a risk score above a defined threshold can be automatically fast-tracked for deployment, while others trigger additional reviews, compensating controls, or specific-use restrictions.We are also working on additional integrations that would make this easier and more extensible for that use!

We also have an AMA session to connect with the community and answer any further questions - feel free to register and attend!https://noma.security/behind-the-riskrubric-ai-algorithm-an-ama-on-transparent-ai-model-risk/.

CNBC reported on November 26, 2026 that Nvidia chip sellers have told neocloud operators, which rent out accelerated computing capacity, they will not supply GPUs if any of the resulting computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, citing two people familiar with the private communications.

The condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the manufacturer had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds.

In a recent development, the disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases.

The seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS said the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments.

The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations.

Aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case.

Exporters and foreign data centers are expected to check customers for direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located or headquartered in those destinations, including through an ultimate parent. A data center’s refusal or inability to provide sufficient compliance information is a red flag that must be resolved before proceeding.

According to recent reports, A later change from a permitted end use to a prohibited one can require BIS authorization. Data centers already providing covered compute before publication must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date to continue without facing future export restrictions.

Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end users that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries.

The reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Under the reported condition, a neocloud’s hardware access depends on the customers its capacity will serve, wherever the data center is located.

AI Could Soon Edit Live Videos in Real Time

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context.
  • Sources indicate that for example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time.
  • According to recent reports, microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context. Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered editing could reshape that connection by changing speech before it reaches viewers.

Sources indicate that for example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time. Such capabilities could support clearer communication, but they also raise questions about whose words audiences actually hear. Understanding the differences between original and AI-edited video can help explain what editable video could mean for viewer trust.

According to recent reports, microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch. Its scope covers both recorded presentations and near-real-time changes to live events. The proposed system could remove filler words, correct mispronunciations and replace other speech, including colloquial expressions or words it identifies as inappropriate. It would also adjust the speaker’s lip movements to match the replacement audio.

In a recent development, audience profiles could influence those choices. The filing describes profiles containing details such as age, language, cultural background and education level, which could guide speech replacements. Viewers could therefore receive different versions of the same event, with wording tailored to their profiles.

The proposed process begins with capturing a speaker’s audio and video during a live event. An AI agent identifies words to change, guided by editing settings or audience profiles. Generative AI then creates replacement speech and adjusts the corresponding video frames, including lip movements, to match.

These changes would happen within a short broadcast buffer. The filing describes a roughly one-to-10-second delay, giving the system time to process speech before presenting the modified stream. To keep the result flowing naturally, the system would smooth audio and visual transitions around each replacement. Some implementations could also patch captions to reflect the edited speech and retain original recordings for later reference.

Recent findings suggest that multilingual presentations could let viewers hear speech in their preferred language while seeing lip movements that match the translation. Educational broadcasts and training sessions could use this approach to reach audiences across language barriers. Audience-based adjustments could also help explain unfamiliar terms in language suited to viewers’ knowledge.

Speakers who stutter could choose to use optional editing support during presentations or live broadcasts. That choice should remain with the speaker, including control over which speech patterns the system changes. Removing a hesitation can make speech easier to follow while preserving the message, although pauses sometimes convey uncertainty or emphasis. Meanwhile, replacing a factual claim changes the substance of the statement and requires a different level of scrutiny and speaker approval.

Existing AI tools already offer parts of the proposed system’s capabilities, including translated speech, synchronized lip movements and live voice modification. Their uses and limitations help show how Microsoft’s proposal compares with available products and research demonstrations.

According to recent reports, heyGen’s Video Translation tool works with uploaded footage, translating speech into a selected language and synchronizing the speaker’s lips with the latest audio. Its Dynamic Duration option lets individual segments stretch or compress by up to 20%, allowing more natural pacing when translations are longer or shorter. This flexibility helps accommodate differences in phrasing between languages.

The workflow processes an existing recording before the creator shares the translated version. Microsoft’s proposed system would instead modify an incoming live broadcast within a short delay, making changes while the event continues.

Krisp’s AI Accent Conversion processes speech during live conversations, adjusting pronunciation to help listeners understand the speaker more easily. It aims to preserve the person’s voice and tone while modifying how words sound. This could support communication in customer service calls and meetings where unfamiliar accents create listening challenges.

The distinction lies in what changes. Accent conversion focuses on pronunciation while preserving the words and their meanings. Microsoft’s proposed system goes further by allowing word replacements and corresponding video edits, potentially changing the statement itself.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s VASA-1 explores how AI can turn a still portrait into a moving, speaking face using an accompanying audio clip. Beyond matching mouth movements to speech, it generates changes in expression and head position that make the face appear more lifelike. It offers another example of how AI can create convincing footage from limited source material.

In a recent development, its ability to animate a portrait also creates opportunities for impersonation, particularly when someone pairs a recognizable face with fabricated speech. Those concerns led Microsoft to withhold public access, with no full release planned until it has confidence in its ability to ensure regulation-compliant use. This position reflects the challenge of making useful avatar technology available while limiting applications that could falsely portray someone saying something.

When AI changes speech while preserving a speaker’s appearance, viewers could attribute the replacement words to that person. A speaker might approve pronunciation corrections without agreeing to changes that reshape an opinion or factual claim. Consent therefore needs to cover the scope of editing, especially when the finished video presents generated words as the speaker’s own.

Generated talking faces and synthetic voices extend this concern beyond alterations to existing footage. They could make someone appear to deliver a statement without participating in the recording. Some people already struggle to recognize sarcasm or identify a skit. When staged content already confuses, the prospect of widespread deepfake misinformation becomes a reasonable concern. Research shows that all age groups are susceptible to digital manipulation.

Industry observers note that convincing impersonations could damage reputations or distort public debate. Their growing plausibility could also give people an excuse to dismiss authentic recordings as AI fabrications, making genuine evidence harder to establish.

Broadcasters and creators should clearly disclose AI edits and provide access to original recordings, especially when changes affect meaning. These steps help audiences understand what changed and give speakers control over statements presented in their name. Independent platforms like C2PA Content Credentials can support transparency by documenting media origins and editing history. They function like a nutrition label for digital content, allowing anyone to inspect the available history using compatible tools.

For consequential clips, viewers should compare the footage with sources and independent reporting. Realistic faces, matching lip movements and familiar voices alone offer limited grounds for trust.

According to recent reports, AI video editing could improve cross-language communication and give speakers more control over how they present themselves. Microsoft’s proposed system and research demonstrations represent different stages of development. As audiovisual edits become more convincing, disclosure and verifiable original recordings will become more important for maintaining trust.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a tech giant that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me.".

In a recent development, the talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain noted the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been.".

According to recent reports, A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain remarked, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

According to recent reports, to replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

Sources indicate that jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

It has been revealed that he closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Gaia2 and ARE: Empowering the community to study agents

📅 22 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants.
  • It has been revealed that that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors.
  • Industry observers note that GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants. When given a query, they would easily manage ambiguity in instructions, construct step-by-step plans, correctly identify necessary resources, execute those plans without getting sidetracked, and adapt to unexpected events, all while maintaining accuracy and avoiding hallucinations. However, developing agents and testing these behaviors is no small feat: if you have ever tried to debug your own agent, you’ve probably observed how tedious and frustrating this can be. Existing evaluation environments are tightly coupled with the tasks they evaluate, lack real-world flexibility, and do not reflect the messy reality of open-world agents: simulated pages never fail to load, events don’t spontaneously emerge, and asynchronous chaos is absent.

It has been revealed that that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors. Gaia2 is released with the open Meta Agents Research Environments (ARE) framework to run, debug and evaluate agents. ARE simulates complex real world-like conditions and can be customized to further study agents behaviors. Gaia2 dataset is released under CC by 4.0 license, and ARE under MIT license.

Industry observers note that GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve. In 2 years, the easiest levels have become too easy for models, and the community is coming close to solving the hardest questions, so it was time for an entirely upcoming and harder agent benchmark!

Here comes Gaia2, a follow up to GAIA, going way beyond it in terms of capabilities studied!

Where GAIA was read-only, Gaia2 is now a read-and-write benchmark, focusing on interactive behavior and complexity management. Agents are now evaluated not only on search and retrieval, but also on instruction following over ambiguous or time-sensitive queries, in a noisy environment with controlled failures - reflecting real-world conditions more than any other simulated environment. We want to test how agents manage tools or APIs that sometimes do not work, plan successions of actions with very specific time frames, and adapt to new events - a whole new range of complexity!

To do this, we use the following task groups (thanks to 1000 brand new human-created scenarios):.

In the spirit of GAIA, scenarios do not require specialized knowledge: humans should in principle be able to get 100%, which allows easy debugging for model developers.

Want to explore the benchmark? Check out our dataset, which you can better display in our demo here.

Gaia2 runs with ARE, an execution environment, where an agent of your choice has access to a combination of applications and associated pre-populated data.

According to recent reports, for Gaia2, we created a smartphone mock-up environment, simulating what a human would use in their daily life. It contains real-world applications such as messaging (Email), utilities (Calendar, Contacts, Shopping, a FileSystem, …), and a chat interface to talk to the agent. All applications are also accessible to the agents through tool calling. Last but not least, the demo also contains a simulated persona’s history of conversations and app interactions.

All agent interactions are automatically recorded as structured traces during execution for deep dives and analysis: they include tool calls, API responses, model thoughts, timing metrics (e.g., response latency), user interactions, and so forth - and can all be exported as JSON.

For reference, we compare a range of large open and closed source models: Llama 3.3-70B Instruct, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B-MoE, Grok-4, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, and GPT-5 in all reasoning modes.

Industry observers note that all models are evaluated using the same setup (a uniform ReAct loop for consistency, temperature of 0.5, generation limit of 16K tokens), with a combination of model-as-a-judge (Llama 3.3 Instruct 70B) and exact-match evaluation depending on the particular task. All 101 tools (and the general environment description) are provided in the system prompt.

Among the evaluated models, the highest-scoring model overall as of September 2025 is GPT-5 with high reasoning, and the best open source model is Kimi K2.

Some capabilities appear to be already close to solved by the best models: execution of simple tool calls and instruction following (execution), and overall search (as we could have guessed from current results on GAIA). The ambiguity, adaptability, and noise splits remain challenging for now for all models, and it’s interesting to see that performance on what were considered complex agentic tasks (instruction following and search) is not a good proxy for performance on closer-to-real-world tasks. Last but not least, the hardest split for all models at the moment is the time one: it’s very hard at this moment for models to correctly handle time-sensitive actions (though this could likely be mitigated by the use of specialised tools and better temporal reasoning). Detailed analysis of these results can be found in the paper.

However, we believe it’s important to push reporting beyond raw scores: if the model is correct but took several thousand tokens to reach the correct solution, or ran for several hours, it is “not as good” as a model which succeeded orders of magnitude faster. We therefore also normalize scores for cost, quantified as the average number of LLM calls and output tokens (which both define a cost-performance Pareto frontier). In the paper you’ll find score vs monetary cost and time.

If you want to evaluate your model on Gaia2, you can follow these steps:.

First, install Meta's Agent Research Environment in your Python environment of choice (uv, conda, virtualenv, ...).

Then, run the benchmark for all configurations: execution, search, adaptability, time and ambiguity. Don't forget to upload all results to the hub with the hf_upload kwarg!

Run the oracle to get your aggregated score file.

Finally, add all the relevant information about your model in the README, and share it on the leaderboard to centralize Gaia2 traces here!

Beyond benchmark scenarios, you can use Gaia2 apps and content in ARE to see if the model is able to correctly solve less verifiable tasks such as loading emails, writing follow-ups, adding events to the calendar or booking meetings - in sum, providing the perfect setup to evaluate your AI assistants through interaction!

You can also easily customise the environment, by 1) connecting your tools (via MCP or directly ) to test your agents on it; 2) implementing your own scenarios, including defining trigger or timed events (eg: after 2 minutes, the Mail app will receive a newly introduced email from Contact), to see how the agent is able to adapt to an evolving environment.

(As the agents are by default json agents, they can’t mess up your machine, unless of course you connect them to external apps with unsafe rights. So, operate with caution when adding your own apps or using untrusted MCPs).

Here are several use cases that we’ve used ARE for:.

We recorded 3 videos so you can check some of these use cases (but of course, we hope the community gets creative with ARE :hugging_face:). For these videos, we use the default demo described above, which contains the simulated life of Linda Renne, PhD student in machine learning.

To test how good the default model is at event organisation, let’s strategy a birthday party!

We first ask the agent to text everyone in the Renne family about the user’s 30th birthday party on November 7. The default universe has 21 contacts in the list, including 5 Renne family members - Linda, the simulation “owner”, George and Stephie, her parents, Anna her sister, and Morgan her grandfather. The agent successfully goes through the contact list, finds the four family members, and texts them.

Recent findings suggest that next, we ask the agent to create a calendar invite and add them as invitees. The agent remembers the above context! It creates a calendar invite on the correct date and correctly adds the family members to it.

According to recent reports, ARE also allows us to check the traces behind the actions taken by the agent. Upon opening the Agent logs tool on the left, we can see the system prompt, the chain of thought, multi-step actions taken with the tools called, and the outcomes as neatly organised logs. Everything can be exported as json if you want to consult things offline!

The Canadian government expanded the AI Compute Access Fund with an additional $700 million on November 26, 2026, bringing it to $1 billion and opening a sector-specific call for health and life sciences projects.

Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced the next phase in Toronto. The expansion adds to the fund’s initial $300 million and is intended to help Canadian organizations develop, test and commercialize AI products by offsetting cloud-compute costs. Eligible work includes model training, inference and fine-tuning.

Industry observers note that solomon also declared more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies. Those earlier-phase awards are distinct from the expansion and cover health care, agriculture, manufacturing, finance and transportation projects.

Sources indicate that the updated program guide covers up to 80% of eligible cloud-compute costs from sovereign providers and up to 50% from Canadian-based providers. Sovereign suppliers must operate infrastructure in Canada, process and store data there, be incorporated and registered in Canada, be Canadian-owned, and keep governance and decision-making authority in the country.

Canadian-based providers must meet the infrastructure, data and incorporation requirements. The ownership and governance tests do not apply to that category. Multinational companies with Canadian-registered entities can therefore qualify when the infrastructure and data remain in Canada. The rate structure offers a larger potential subsidy for choosing a provider with Canadian ownership and control without excluding multinational suppliers’ Canadian operations.

It has been revealed that eligible proposals must include $100,000 to $5 million in compute costs and end no later than March 31, 2030. Applicants can be Canadian-registered for-profit companies, nonprofit corporations or charities, including qualifying postsecondary institutions; they generally need fewer than 500 full-time-equivalent employees, Canada-based research and development teams and a commercialization proposal. Contributions may be non-repayable, conditionally repayable or repayable, depending on the project’s assessed benefits and risk.

Health and life sciences applicants must submit a statement of interest by 11:59 p.m. ET on December 17, 2026. Those invited to proceed must file full applications by 11:59 p.m. ET on January 4, 2027, with compute contracts, invoices or other documentation in place or in progress. A selected applicant whose agreement is still in progress must finalize it before signing a contribution agreement.

It has been revealed that assessment covers market potential, organizational and financial capacity, technology readiness, expected economic and public benefits, and alignment with government priorities. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada states it will endeavour to make funding decisions within 90 business days after the call closes. The department will also use AI tools to support analysis of application information, conduct risk-related research and assist with program administration, while retaining final authority over recipient selection.

An official recipient backgrounder highlights the range of supported work. Vancouver-based Apera AI is developing 4D vision and simulation-driven models for factory robots, while Toronto-based RetiSpec is working on a non-invasive retinal-imaging tool intended to detect early Alzheimer’s disease. Gotcare, also in Toronto, is building an AI-enabled home-healthcare management system focused on rural and underserved populations.

The sector calls sit within the government’s AI for All strategy, which names five priority areas: health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing and robotics. The strategy describes Canada’s sovereign compute capacity as nascent and says most Canadian small and medium-sized businesses lack an affordable domestic option, leaving them reliant on foreign cloud platforms for training, testing and deployment.

Sources indicate that the government is also connecting the renewed fund to its commitment to bring 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute online. The expanded program is intended to create demand for Canadian providers and support investment in domestic AI infrastructure, linking commercialization assistance to a broader infrastructure objective.

That makes the reimbursement gap central to the policy: companies receive the strongest support when their computing is owned, operated and governed in Canada. The open question is whether the demand created by these subsidies can support enough affordable domestic capacity while helping Canadian AI products reach the market.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A backtest gives you a number: total PnL, Sharpe, max drawdown.
  • According to recent reports, consider two strategies with identical trade lists: same 300 trades, same total PnL, same win rate.
  • A Monte Carlo permutation test fixes this cheaply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A backtest gives you a number: total PnL, Sharpe, max drawdown. The first two are (roughly) order-independent if you're just summing returns. Max drawdown is not. Neither is the probability that your equity curve touches a ruin threshold before the backtest window ends.

According to recent reports, consider two strategies with identical trade lists: same 300 trades, same total PnL, same win rate. One sequence happens to cluster its losses early and its wins late. The other does the reverse. Same totals, radically different drawdowns, radically different risk of blowing up mid-stream. Your backtest only sampled one of the possible orderings — the one that actually happened, or worse, the one your optimization pipeline selected for.

A Monte Carlo permutation test fixes this cheaply. Shuffle the realized trade PnL sequence thousands of times, recompute max drawdown and ruin indicators on every shuffle, then look at the resulting distribution. If your backtest's drawdown sits at the 5th percentile of the shuffled distribution, your headline number is flattering you. If it sits near the median, the strategy's risk is roughly order-neutral and you can trust the backtest more.

It has been revealed that the key assumption: the multiset of trade PnLs is fixed, only the order is random. This tests sensitivity to sequencing, not to whether the trades themselves were lucky. It's a stress audit of path risk, not a validation of edge.

Assume you have a vector of per-trade PnL in account currency (or in R-multiples — the math is identical, only the ruin thresholds change units).

The permutation test only cares about the values, not their original order. If you want to audit the actual backtest drawdown, keep the original array around — you'll compare it against the shuffled distribution.

Sources indicate that the naive approach loops over 5000 shuffles in Python and calls np.cumsum each time. That's fine for 300 trades but painful at 5000 trades × 5000 shuffles. Vectorize it: build a matrix of shape (n_sims, n_trades), cumsum along axis 1, then compute running max and drawdown per row.

It has been revealed that for 5000 trades and 5000 simulations, that's a 25M-element float64 array — about 200 MB. If memory is tight, chunk the simulations:.

It has been revealed that max drawdown is one number per shuffle. Ruin probability is the fraction of shuffles where the equity curve drops below a threshold at any point. Compute it directly from the drawdown matrix — no extra pass needed.

In a recent development, pass thresholds in the same units as your PnL. If you're sizing in R-multiples and risking 1% of equity per trade, a 20R drawdown is roughly a 20% equity hit (ignoring compounding). Pick thresholds that map to real operational limits: margin call levels, a hard stop-loss on the strategy, a psychological "I'd shut this down" number.

In a recent development, sometimes you want this in a script with no numpy dependency — a research notebook on a locked-down box, a quick check in a CI step, or a port to another language. The pure-Python version is 20 lines and fast enough for a few hundred trades.

random.Random.shuffle mutates the list in place, so you don't rebuild it every iteration — that's the main cost saver. If you need ruin probabilities too, track the minimum equity inside the loop and collect it. For 1000 trades × 5000 sims this takes a few seconds; the numpy version is roughly 50–100× faster.

It has been revealed that now the part that actually matters. You have a distribution of 5000 max drawdowns. What do you do with it?

The percentile of your backtest DD tells you how flattering the realized order was. A backtest DD at the 10th percentile means 90% of orderings produce a worse drawdown — the strategy's risk is understated. At the 50th, you're unbiased. At the 90th, your backtest was unusually unlucky and the strategy is probably better than it looks (rare, but it happens with short samples).

A concrete rule that works in practice:.

Sources indicate that one caveat worth stating plainly: this test assumes trade PnLs are exchangeable. Real strategies have autocorrelation — volatility clustering, regime shifts, correlated losses during stress. Permutation tests ignore that, so they can understate tail drawdowns when losses cluster. If you suspect serial dependence, the permutation test is a lower bound on path risk, not an upper one. Combine it with a block bootstrap or a regime-conditional analysis if the strategy is sensitive to volatility regimes.

It tells you whether your backtest drawdown is representative of the drawdown distribution over all orderings of the same trades. It does not tell you whether the trades themselves are predictive, whether the sample is large enough, or whether the strategy will work out of sample. Those are separate questions with separate tests.

In a recent development, what it does well: it catches the specific failure mode where a strategy looks safe because the backtest got a lucky ordering. That failure mode is common, cheap to test for, and expensive to discover live. Five thousand shuffles and a percentile lookup is a small price.

We release all training recipes, data-processing tools, resulting model, demo and datasets to enable full reproducibility and foster further research 🫡. Find the collection here.

Graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision. Developing models that see and interact with user interfaces enables AI agents to navigate mobile, desktop, and web platforms. This will reshape the future of digital interaction.

Industry observers note that in this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy. We demonstrate how to transform a model with zero grounding capabilities into an agentic coder capable of understanding and interacting with graphical interfaces.

Rather than aiming for a SOTA model, our goal is to demonstrate the entire process, from data processing to model training, and, in doing so, show how to unlock GUI-grounding capabilities in VLMs.

GUI capabilities combine understanding of the interface and precise element localization. These abilities enable the model to translate high-level tasks into low-level GUI actions such as clicking, typing, ….

Sources indicate that our approach leverages SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct as the baseline model, a small powerful vision-language model that initially has no grounding capabilities for GUI tasks. This makes it an ideal candidate to demonstrate the effectiveness of our training methodology. Through our two-phase training process, we first instill grounding capabilities in the model, then enhance it with agentic reasoning abilities using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

Sources indicate that we evaluate our approach on an established perception benchmark: ScreenSpot-v2, which tests the model’s ability to understand and locate elements within screenshots. Our process is inspired by the AGUVIS paper, and we leverage their carefully curated datasets to build upon their foundational work.

Evolution of ScreenSpot-v2 performance during the training phase of the base model SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct.

According to recent reports, this section explains how we convert heterogeneous GUI actions format from multiple datasets into a single unified format. By standardizing function names, signatures, and parameters, we create consistent, high-quality data that forms the foundation for effective model training.

Sources indicate that one of the primary challenges when working with multiple GUI automation datasets is the lack of standardization in action representations. Different datasets use varying function signatures, parameter naming conventions, and action taxonomies, making it difficult to train a unified model across diverse data sources.

We took the open-source datasets (xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2), originally used by AGUVIS, and implemented a comprehensive data transformation pipeline to create a unified action space. Our approach involved:.

This unification process was essential for creating coherent training data that allows the model to learn consistent action patterns across diverse GUI environments.

To maximize flexibility for different use cases, we developed the Action Space Converter (utils/action_space_converter.py), a tool that allows people to easily adapt from an action space to their own custom action vocabularies and naming conventions.

You can use this tool to transform one action signature (function names, parameter names, and parameter value changes, ...) into another:.

The Action Space Converter provides:.

This tool enables researchers and practitioners to:.

The Action Space Converter is particularly valuable for preparing datasets for training, as it ensures consistent action vocabularies across different deployment environments while maintaining compatibility with existing automation frameworks.

It has been revealed that through this pipeline, we transform the open-source datasets xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2 into our unified action space (see here). The output of this process is released as two new fully formatted datasets: smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 and smolagents/aguvis-stage-2.

Phase 1 leverages the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset, which introduces GUI grounding by pairing low-level instructions with diverse executable actions (expressed in code form). For example, a user/assistant turn in smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 follows the structure:.

In a recent development, each sample links a screenshot with multi-turn user/assistant interactions, enabling the model to learn fine-grained action grounding across dialogue turns. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Before proceeding with full-scale Phase 1 training, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to determine optimal training configurations.

We experimented with different image sizes and coordinate representation systems to identify the optimal configuration for SmolVLM2:.

Some SOTA GUI VLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL) appear also to use a different normalized range (0–1000), which was not tested in this experiment.

Recent findings suggest that table 1: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (400k samples, aguvis-stage-1). Higher is better.

According to recent reports, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct base initially achieved 0% performance on perception benchmarks like ScreenSpot-v2. This complete lack of grounding capability provided us with a clean slate to evaluate the effectiveness of our training methodology.

From our experiments, we determined that:.

Using the optimal configuration (1152px resolution with normalized coordinates), we trained for 2 epochs on the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset. The results were remarkable, +41% improvement over baseline on ScreenSpot-v2.

This dramatic improvement demonstrates that our Phase 1 training successfully instilled fundamental grounding capabilities in the model, enabling it to understand and locate visual elements within screenshots.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

Whereas Phase 1 provided grounding capabilities, Phase 2 targets agentic reasoning, the ability to deliberate and plan before acting. This stage transforms the model from a reactive system identifying GUI elements into a proactive agent capable of executing complex, multi-step interactions.

Phase 2 uses the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 dataset, which introduces agentic scenarios:.

Explicit reasoning about upcoming actions.

Context consistency across multiple interaction steps.

High-level instructions require multi-step, low-level actions.

For example, the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 chat message is like this:.

Each sample links a screenshot with a system/user/assistant turn. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Starting from the Phase 1 checkpoint (1152 px resolution, normalized coordinates), we fine-tuned the model for two epochs on smolagents/aguvis-stage-2. The accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 increased from 41% to 61%, indicating that explicit reasoning improves GUI grounding performance.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct after Phase 1 finetuning (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

All training code, data processing pipelines, datasets and model are open-source!

Recent findings suggest that our experiments demonstrate that high-quality, reasoning-oriented data can substantially improve GUI grounding, even for small VLMs, using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Beyond raw performance gains, these results show that the GUI grounding capabilities are largely determined by the quality of the data. Carefully curated datasets teach models the structure and semantics of user interfaces, providing the grounding needed for accurate action prediction.

To support the development of GUI agents, we’re open-sourcing everything: our complete pipeline, datasets, and trained model. You can reproduce our results, experiment with different models and architectures, or adapt our approach to fresh domains. The future of agentic AI depends on researchers like you pushing these boundaries further!

While SFT excels at supervised tasks, emerging methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) help develop stronger reasoning capabilities and enable real-time adaptation. These advances point toward a new generation of GUI agents that learn and improve through interaction rather than relying solely on static datasets.

Let’s build the future of GUI agents together 🤗.

Python TXT Proof for Logistics Workspace Auto-Join (Evidence Retention)

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev
