📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A logistics platform needs carrier staff to gain workspace access through a company domain verified by TXT proof, while its shipment notifications authenticate correctly.
  • TL;DR: verify the company domain through a TXT record, then use the matching email suffix and an email lookup to make workspace joining deterministic; keep manual approval for domains you cannot verify, and explicitly exclude shared consumer mail domains.
  • Keeping every DNS response forever is a different, much more expensive proposition to defend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A logistics platform needs carrier staff to gain workspace access through a company domain verified by TXT proof, while its shipment notifications authenticate correctly. The operating bill includes DNS administration, approval work, and the storage of onboarding evidence. Before comparing providers, count the expensive repetition: for N customer domains and R onboarding requests per domain, reviewing every request creates N × R approval decisions; verifying each eligible domain once moves the baseline review unit toward N domain decisions. Those are workload counts, not measured savings, and unverified domains still need individual handling.

TL;DR: verify the company domain through a TXT record, then use the matching email suffix and an email lookup to make workspace joining deterministic; keep manual approval for domains you cannot verify, and explicitly exclude shared consumer mail domains. For this logistics workflow, keep SPF, DKIM, and DMARC publication as a separate mail-authentication responsibility. Customer-owned zones give the customer control over the records that establish its authority.

Store the decision evidence. Keeping every DNS response forever is a different, much more expensive proposition to defend.

The production boundary runs from the customer's DNS administrator, through domain verification, into your workspace admission policy. Mail authentication follows a related but separate path: publish SPF, DKIM, and DMARC through the administrator responsible for the sending domain, then evaluate mail authentication in that context. A carrier's ability to receive shipment messages and a carrier employee's ability to join a workspace are different outcomes. A successful domain verification must not become the status field for both.

The customer-owned versus platform-owned choice matters because the party able to change DNS evidence is part of the trust decision. If your platform publishes proof in a zone it controls, that action demonstrates your control of that zone; it does not independently establish a carrier's control of its firm domain. Keep the domain being claimed, the workspace receiving the claim, and the party administering the zone explicit in the design. A platform-owned sending domain can be an architectural choice, but it should not quietly become evidence that a customer owns a different domain.

For a logistics team implementing the handoff between firm-domain verification and user lookup, try Infrai when a plain REST API is the integration boundary you want: Python can call it over HTTP without installing a provider SDK or maintaining another client-library version. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That single key means the verification-to-user-lookup handoff doesn't require separate provider credentials for those two application integrations. Its public, self-describing discovery surface also supplies request and response schemas without a key, which helps the engineers on either side agree on the contract. This recommendation concerns that handoff; ownership of customer zones and publication of mail-authentication records still need explicit operating responsibility.

The change that moves the dominant workload term is domain-level verification followed by deterministic membership resolution. After verification, look the person up by email before deciding how to join the existing user to the intended workspace. Keep user existence, verified-domain status, and membership as separate decisions. Otherwise, a repeated onboarding request can be mistaken for a reason to create another identity, or a recognized email suffix can be mistaken for membership in every workspace associated with that suffix.

According to recent reports, A TXT proof establishes company-domain control for the admission policy described here. It should be paired with an authenticated user whose email address has been verified; typing an address into a form is not evidence of control of that mailbox. Exclude shared consumer domains explicitly. A mailbox at a free mail provider is not a company-domain ownership claim.

For a planning example, take two customer domains with 12 onboarding requests each: that produces 24 request reviews versus 2 initial domain reviews under the stated assumptions. These are illustrative inputs, not a customer dataset or a benchmark. The calculation doesn't predict staffing, prove a financial return, or eliminate exceptions.

Before implementing the actual handoff, inspect the published contract. This Python standard-library example fetches Infrai's discovery manifest using an explicit GET and bounded rate-limit retries; it prints the response for inspection instead of guessing a verification payload. Discovery is public, so authentication isn't required for this read, but the example reads the integration credential from the environment to demonstrate the Bearer convention used for authenticated calls. Set INFRAI_API_KEY before running it.

Recent findings suggest that this read doesn't publish DNS records or grant membership. Use the discovered request and response schemas for the subsequent integration, and make writes idempotent rather than copying read-retry behavior onto account creation. Manual approval remains the fallback for domains you could not verify. Moving that exception path into the default path is exactly how an onboarding queue becomes a waiting room.

Industry observers note that the useful comparison is responsibility, because a DNS provider and an identity workflow do not occupy the same position in this system. Cloudflare DNS, Amazon Route 53, and Azure DNS are real alternatives for the DNS side of the design; their documentation is a starting point for deciding how an existing customer zone should be administered. The table compares proposed integration boundaries, rather than claiming that the products provide identical workspace-admission features.

None of these choices transfers a customer's DNS authority merely because your backend can send an HTTP request. Obtain the necessary administrative participation, and decide which party publishes the mail records before presenting onboarding as complete.

Keep the existing DNS provider when it already fits. The reason to add a shared API surface is a concrete reduction in integration contracts around verification and identity, not a reason to migrate every carrier's zone.

In a recent development, for a proposed evidence policy, retain the claimed domain, workspace binding, verification decision, decision time, and the policy version that interpreted it. These are application-owned audit fields, not claims about any provider's response schema. Retain enough user-resolution evidence to explain which verified email led to the membership decision, while treating that information as access-controlled customer data. The retention question is whether an operator can reconstruct the authorization decision, rather than whether the system can accumulate a complete history of DNS observations.

A useful storage model is D × E × T: domains under management, evidence collected per domain per interval, and retained intervals. This is an accounting model, not a measured storage bill. Reducing retained observations changes E or T; changing which customers own their zones does not automatically change either one. Keep the decision record longer than disposable observation details if the support and audit requirements justify that distinction. Set the actual periods against those requirements rather than copying a generic number of days.

Recent findings suggest that name the failures before choosing retention. A stale ownership decision means the old evidence no longer describes current control. A wrong workspace binding means valid domain evidence was attached to the wrong tenant. An ambiguous email lookup means identity resolution has not produced a deterministic user. A shared-domain admission error means a consumer email suffix was treated as tech giant authority. These are application design risks, and each requires a different piece of evidence; a large archive of TXT responses cannot repair a missing workspace binding.

Mail adds a separate diagnostic question. A DMARC investigation concerns mail authentication and policy, so the evidence relevant to it must not be replaced with a workspace verification flag. RFC 7489 is the reference for that protocol boundary. Do not promise delivery merely because a carrier's staff can now sign in.

The practical default is customer-domain TXT verification, email-based lookup, and automatic joining for eligible matching addresses, with manual approval for unverified domains. Use a direct DNS provider when zone administration is the principal job; consider a shared REST surface when verification and identity handoff create the extra integration work. Keep mail authentication visible as its own completion condition.

In a recent development, the deliberate deletion is repetitive raw DNS observations after their diagnostic retention period, while preserving the decision record for the period your access-review obligations require. That sacrifices the ability to replay every earlier observation during a later dispute. Recovery may require fresh domain proof and another conversation with the customer's DNS administrator; the retained decision should still explain why access was granted at the time. Accept that cost explicitly. Otherwise, retention becomes an unbounded substitute for a recovery plan.

Most of the time people use the Tokenizers or Hub modules, and frequently both. Some notable projects that rely on swift-transformers include:.

Version 1.0 signals stability in the package. Developers are building apps on swift-transformers, and this first major release recognizes those use cases and brings the version number in line with that reality. It also provides the foundation on which to iterate with the community to build the next set of features. These are some of our preferred updates:.

Recent findings suggest that version 1.0 comes with breaking API changes. However, we don’t expect major problems if you are a user of Tokenizers or Hub. If you use the Core ML components of the library, please get in touch so we can support you during transition. We’ll prepare a migration guide and add it to the documentation.

Honestly, we don’t know. We are thinking along the lines of better integration with mlx-swift-examples for LLMs and VLMs, potentially through pre-processing and post-processing operations that developers encounter frequently.

Industry observers note that we are also extremely excited about agentic use in general and MCP in particular. We think that exposure of system resources to local workflows would be 🚀.

If you want to follow along in this journey or want to share your ideas, please contact us through our social networks or the repo.

Industry observers note that we are immensely grateful to all the contributors and people of the library for your help and feedback. We love you all, and can't wait to continue working with you to shape the future of on-device generation! ❤️.

Tech Report: Correcting Sharpe Ratios for Autocorrelation: The Lo Factor in Practice

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Sharpe ratio's standard error formula assumes i.i.d.
  • The fix is cheap: correct the Sharpe ratio by the Lo factor before you run any significance test.
  • Sources indicate that lo (2002) derives the asymptotic variance of the Sharpe estimator under serial dependence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sharpe ratio's standard error formula assumes i.i.d. returns. That assumption is almost always false for real strategies: smoothed marks, overlapping holding periods, illiquid positions, and momentum effects all leave a lag-1 autocorrelation in the return series. When returns are autocorrelated, the effective sample size is smaller than the nominal one, and significance tests fire far too often. With rho = 0.2, a nominal 5% test rejects the null at 18–25% in simulation. That is not a small calibration error; it is the difference between "maybe real" and "coin flip.".

The fix is cheap: correct the Sharpe ratio by the Lo factor before you run any significance test.

Sources indicate that lo (2002) derives the asymptotic variance of the Sharpe estimator under serial dependence. For an AR(1)-style dependence with lag-1 autocorrelation rho, the corrected Sharpe is:.

The rule I use: apply the correction whenever |rho| > 0.1. Below that threshold the adjustment is within noise of the estimate itself, and applying it adds churn without information. Above it, ignoring the correction is a methodological error, not a modeling choice.

The (1 - rho)/(1 + rho) factor is the AR(1) special case. For q-th order dependence, the full Lo variance uses a weighted sum of autocorrelations:.

For most daily-frequency strategies, lag-1 dominates and the closed form above is enough. Use the general form when you have overlapping windows (e.g., 5-day returns sampled daily), where lag-k dependence out to k = 4 is structural, not noise.

Do not eyeball this from a chart. Compute it, and compute it on the return series you actually test, not on cumulative PnL. Cumulative PnL is a random walk under the null and will show high autocorrelation regardless of the strategy.

Two practical checks before you trust the number:.

Keep the correction in one place so every downstream test uses the same number.

Then wire it into your evaluation path:.

The SharpeReport object carries both numbers and a flag. Log the flag. If a strategy's headline Sharpe only survives because the correction was never applied, you want that visible in the report, not buried in a notebook.

Industry observers note that the point estimate correction is what people remember, but the test is where the false positives come from. The corrected Sharpe has standard error approximately:.

Sources indicate that note the direction: positive autocorrelation inflates the standard error by the same factor that deflates the point estimate. Both effects push you toward "not significant," which is the honest conclusion. A quick t-statistic:.

Run this on raw and corrected Sharpe with the same rho and the same n. If the raw version clears 3.0 and the corrected one does not, the strategy does not clear 3.0.

Negative autocorrelation is the less-discussed case, and it is worth walking through because the correction moves the number up, which invites overconfidence.

Suppose a mean-reversion strategy on a liquid futures contract shows an annualized Sharpe of 1.40 over 500 daily observations, with lag-1 autocorrelation of -0.33. That is a large negative value. Check it against the ACF before proceeding:.

Recent findings suggest that the pattern — strong lag-1, weak lag-2, near-zero beyond — is consistent with a genuine AR(1) mean-reverting component rather than an artifact. Now apply the correction:.

Recent findings suggest that A Sharpe of 1.40 becomes 1.97. That is a 41% uplift, and it is legitimate under the AR(1) model: negative dependence means each observation carries more independent information than its index suggests, so the effective sample is larger than 500.

But the standard error moves too:.

Recent findings suggest that with rho = -0.33, the SE factor is sqrt(0.67 / 1.33) ≈ 0.71, so the standard error shrinks by about 29%. The t-statistic rises, but not by the 41% the point estimate suggests. The two adjustments partially offset. This is the honest reading: negative autocorrelation helps, but less than the headline correction implies.

Two caveats on negative rho specifically:.

The autocorrelation correction is the single most common missing step in strategy evaluation, and it interacts badly with multiple testing.

It has been revealed that consider a grid search over 200 parameter combinations. You keep the best in-sample Sharpe. Two things then compound:.

In a recent development, the result is a strategy that looks significant at p < 0.01 on the raw numbers and is pure noise. The autocorrelation correction does not fix selection bias on its own, but it is a prerequisite. Deflating a Sharpe that was never corrected for dependence deflates the wrong quantity.

A minimal evaluation harness that handles both:.

According to recent reports, the expected_max_z line is a crude proxy for the multiple-testing hurdle, not a substitute for a proper deflated Sharpe. It is there to make the point concrete: once you correct for rho, the bar the best candidate must clear goes up, and the number of candidates that clear it goes down. Usually to zero, which is the correct answer for most grid searches.

Latest Update: The Drawdown Breaker Blind Spot: Realized PnL Hides Unrealized Bleeding

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most drawdown guards are built on a simple, reasonable-sounding premise: track losses, and when losses pile up, stop trading.
  • The problem is that this guard is blind to the exact moment it matters most: while positions are open and bleeding.
  • This post dissects the blind spot, walks through a scenario where every guard reads fine while the account is drowning, and presents a dual-viewport design: realized drawdown and pool-wide mark-to-market unrealized PnL tracked separately, with the unrealized view gating new entries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most drawdown guards are built on a simple, reasonable-sounding premise: track losses, and when losses pile up, stop trading. The implementation almost always looks at the same number — realized PnL. A trade closes, the result is booked, the counter increments. Three losses in a row? Cool off. Daily loss limit hit? Flatten and stop.

The problem is that this guard is blind to the exact moment it matters most: while positions are open and bleeding. An unrealized loss of 4% sitting in three open positions is invisible to a realized-PnL guard. The counter still reads zero. Every safety number is green. Then the positions close — and the drawdown "suddenly" appears, fully formed, in one tick of the counter.

This post dissects the blind spot, walks through a scenario where every guard reads fine while the account is drowning, and presents a dual-viewport design: realized drawdown and pool-wide mark-to-market unrealized PnL tracked separately, with the unrealized view gating new entries.

Consider a typical consecutive-loss breaker:.

Sources indicate that this code is correct for what it measures. The problem is what it doesn't measure. on_trade_closed only fires when a trade closes. Between the open and the close, consecutive_losses and realized_pnl_today are frozen. If you have five positions open and all five are down 1.5% each, the breaker sees zero losses, zero realized drawdown, and happily approves a sixth entry.

The guard is not wrong. It is answering a different question than the one you think you're asking. "How much have I lost?" and "How much am I currently down?" are different quantities, and the gap between them is where accounts die.

It's not laziness. Realized PnL is easy: it's a single scalar that updates on a discrete event. Unrealized PnL is a moving target that requires a mark price per position, updates continuously, and has to handle stale quotes, funding, and partial fills. The realized-only guard is the 80% solution that ships in an afternoon. It's just missing the 20% that contains the worst days.

Industry observers note that here's the concrete version. Suppose the account is 100,000 units of quote currency, the consecutive-loss breaker is set to 3, and the daily loss limit is 2%. Position sizing is 20,000 notional per entry, so a 1.5% adverse move on a position is a 300-unit unrealized loss (0.3% of equity).

09:30 — Two positions open. Both drift against you. Unrealized: −600. Realized today: 0. consecutive_losses: 0. Breaker: open for business.

10:15 — The market trends against the book. A third and fourth position open (the breaker approved them, because nothing has closed). Unrealized across four positions: −2,400 (2.4% of equity). Realized today: still 0. consecutive_losses: still 0. can_open_new returns True.

11:00 — A fifth entry. Unrealized: −3,600. The daily loss limit is 2%, but it's computed on realized PnL, so it reads 0%. The breaker is structurally incapable of firing.

According to recent reports, 13:00 — Stops trigger across the book in a correlated move. All five close within twenty minutes. Realized today: −3,900. consecutive_losses: 5. The breaker finally fires — after the entire drawdown has been realized, and after it approved two entries during the bleed.

At 11:00, the account was down 3.6% on a mark-to-market basis. Every guard reported it was down 0%. The pool was drowning while the dashboard showed a calm surface. This is the blind spot: the guard's measurement point (trade close) is downstream of the risk event (adverse mark-to-market drift on open exposure).

It has been revealed that the design change is to stop treating "drawdown" as one number. Track two:.

The realized view answers "how bad has it been?" The unrealized view answers "how bad is it right now?" Entries should require both to be acceptable.

The mark-to-market gate is checked on entry, not on a timer. You don't need a background thread recomputing the pool every millisecond. You need the check to run at the one moment it can still do something: before a newly introduced order goes out. If the pool is down 1.6% and the cap is 1.5%, the next entry is refused — regardless of what the realized counter indicates.

The two limits are separate knobs with separate meanings. max_unrealized_dd is typically tighter than the realized limit, because unrealized losses are still recoverable and you want to stop adding risk early. max_realized_dd can be looser, because realized losses are sunk and the response there is cooldown, not prevention. Conflating them into one number forces a bad compromise.

Sources indicate that the obvious pushback: mark-to-market is noisy, and a tight unrealized cap will block entries on harmless intraday wicks. Two mitigations, both cheap:.

Feed SmoothedMark.update(price) into guard.mark(symbol, smoothed) and the gate becomes resistant to single-tick noise while still tracking real adverse drift.

The guard change fixes the behavior; you also want the diagnostic so you can see the blind spot forming. Log both viewports on every entry decision, and log the gap:.

The gap column is the interesting one. When realized_dd − unrealized_dd grows large and negative — realized flat, unrealized deeply negative — you are inside the blind spot of a realized-only guard. If you ever run a realized-only breaker in parallel (legacy system, comparison study), this log tells you exactly how many entries it approved that the dual-viewport guard would have refused, and what those entries cost on a mark-to-market basis.

Sources indicate that be clear about the scope. The unrealized gate does not prevent the first position from going against you, and it does not replace per-position stops. It addresses one specific failure mode: the guard that approves fresh risk while existing risk is already underwater. Correlation is the amplifier here — five positions that all bleed together look like five independent decisions to the entry logic and like one concentrated bet to the mark-to-market pool. The pool view catches that; the per-trade view never will.

The general principle generalizes beyond drawdown breakers: any risk control whose measurement event is downstream of the risk event has a blind window. Realized PnL is downstream of unrealized PnL. Trade close is downstream of trade open. The fix is always the same — measure at the point where the risk actually lives, and gate at the point where you can still act.

Breaking: VibeGame: Exploring Vibe Coding Games

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People are trying to vibe code games.
  • I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.
  • It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

First, what is vibe coding? It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".

However, since then, it's used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just "using AI when coding" to "not thinking about the code at all". In this blog post, I'll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what's going on under the hood, but doesn't necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

Earlier I mentioned that "as the project grows, things begin to fall apart". This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very quickly.

To address this matter, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

I couldn't find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn't rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:.

Industry observers note that anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model's context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

Industry observers note that I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

According to recent reports, the official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

Sources indicate that roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it's in-house at Roblox.

In a recent development, the unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

Unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

It has been revealed that this approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:.

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

In a recent development, this will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

Here's the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

However, there are still some major caveats:.

Industry observers note that so, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot "make me a game" approach, it doesn't work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires users to understand the engine's capabilities and limitations.

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:.

Then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

According to recent reports, the engine is at the moment very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

It's also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We're also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

Follow me to keep up with what's going on in the space!

Sources indicate that for anyone interested in exploring what's already being built, we've been collecting the best AI-Assisted and vibe-coded games on VibeTopList. Feel free to check for yourself https://vibetoplist.com/.

I've been working on something along similar lines, called Rosh.

It has been revealed that it covers some of the things you list as missing. Rooms are multiplayer and live: people and AI agents can be in the same room changing it together. The same room works in real time in your browser (three.js), a terminal, Unity and Unreal Engine. It also reads the room back to the AI as text, with notes on what looks wrong, so agents can fix their own object placement etc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi all, this is the sixth post in a small series about the Amazon main image rules that actually get listings suppressed. The first covered the full preflight check list, the second covered source resolution, the third covered frame fill, the fourth was a teardown of a sneaker photo failing three ways, and the fifth was about the content rules no report can check. This one is about reading the report itself.

According to recent reports, A preflight report is only useful if you know what each line is measuring, and what to do when a line is not green. So here is a real report from the tool, line by line, on a real photo: a ceramic mug shot on a beige background.

It has been revealed that the pair below is a real output from the tool, from the examples on the site. Before: the mug on a beige background, and the product only covered 31 percent of the original frame. After: only the product, background removed and composited on exact pure white RGB 255,255,255, centered at 85 percent frame fill, rebuilt at 2000x2000.

Industry observers note that the report marked the photo PASS overall. But PASS overall is not the whole story. Here is every line, and what it means.

It has been revealed that the report found the product and isolated it from the background. The bounding box covered 31 percent of the original frame, which is why the before photo looks small and lost: the camera was too far away, and the frame was mostly beige wall.

Recent findings suggest that what FAIL would look like here: no clear product found, because the photo is a flat lay of five items, or the product blends into a background of the same color. The fix is a reshoot with the product alone in the frame, on a background that contrasts with it.

The output is 2000x2000px, which is the size Amazon wants for zoom. This line is about the delivered file, not your source photo. A tool that outputs 1000px will fail this line no matter how good your source was.

Industry observers note that all 8 edge and corner samples came back pure white. This is the line most sellers skip, and the one that quietly suppresses listings: a background that looks white on your screen can sample at 250 or 247 at the edges, and that is not pure white. The report samples the edges because that is where a leftover tint hides.

What FAIL would look like here: a warm gray cast from indoor lighting, or a soft shadow the background removal left behind. The fix is a clean cutout composited on exact 255,255,255, not a brightness slider pushed until it looks white.

Delivered as .jpg. Amazon main images must be JPEG, so a PNG or WebP output fails this line even if everything else is perfect.

This is the most interesting line in the whole report. The source photo was 900x900px, and it was upscaled to 2000px. The report marked it WARN, not FAIL, because 900px is above the 500px floor where a source fails outright, but below the 2000px that would be sharp at full size.

WARN means: this image will pass, but it will not be as sharp as a photo shot at 2000px or more. If this is your hero image, the one buyers see first, reshoot it at full resolution. If it is a secondary angle and the budget is spent, a WARN is acceptable and you can ship it.

Industry observers note that the rule behind the line: a source under 500px on the longest side fails, because no upscaling can invent the detail Amazon's zoom needs. That was the whole second post in this series.

The product's longest side fills 85 percent of the frame, centered. This is the line the third post in this series was about: Amazon wants the product to dominate the frame, and the original 31 percent bounding box is exactly why the before photo would never have worked as a main image.

Read it in this order. First, fix any FAIL, because a FAIL is a rule broken. Second, read the WARN lines and decide whether the photo matters enough to reshoot. Third, remember what the report cannot see: the content rules from the last post, text, props, lifestyle elements, watermarks. A report that is all green still needs your eyes on the frame.

And one habit that saves the most time: never edit the report to make it green. If the background line fails, fix the photo, not the file. A report you faked will not protect the listing, and Amazon checks the image, not your PDF.

The checks are technical only: pure white background, 2000x2000 JPEG output, frame fill, and source resolution. Content rules stay with the seller. A PASS report means the technical rules passed, not that the image is compliant.

If you have a suppressed listing right now, I am happy to run one photo through the preflight and show you the report, free, in the comments. Tell me which line you are unsure about, and we can work out what it means for your photo.

Tool: https://mainimagepass.site.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

It has been revealed that qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

Speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

Before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

According to recent reports, the speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Our recent work indicates that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

Recent findings suggest that the resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

To showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

In our demo, we assigned the accelerated Qwen3-based agent a task: 👉 Summarize the key features of the Qwen3 model series and present them in a slide deck.

Here’s how it worked: 1. The agent used a web search tool to gather up-to-date information. 2. It then switched to the Python interpreter to generate slides with the python-pptx library. This simple workflow highlights just a fraction of the possibilities unlocked when accelerated Qwen3 models meet frameworks like 🤗smolagents, bringing practical, efficient AI agents to life on AI PC. Try it here 🚀.

Gate.io API Pagination Trap: from+to+limit Cannot Coexist

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you've wired up Gate.io's futures candlestick endpoint, you've probably hit this: you build a request with a start time, an end time, and a page size, and the server replies HTTP 400.
  • Here's the endpoint in question (USDT-margined perpetual futures):.
  • The rule the docs bury: from, to, and limit are mutually constrained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you've wired up Gate.io's futures candlestick endpoint, you've probably hit this: you build a request with a start time, an end time, and a page size, and the server replies HTTP 400. You strip out to, retry, and it works. You add it back, it breaks. The error message doesn't mention to at all — it usually complains about something generic like an invalid parameter or an empty result set, which sends you chasing the wrong thing for an hour.

Here's the endpoint in question (USDT-margined perpetual futures):.

Query parameters that matter for history:.

The rule the docs bury: from, to, and limit are mutually constrained. from+limit works. from+to works. to+limit works. All three together returns 400. And there's a second constraint that bites later: any single call returns at most the most recent 10,000 data points, regardless of how wide your range is.

It has been revealed that let's pin down the failure so it's not folklore. The code below is the minimal reproduction — no retry logic, no abstractions.

The message varies and is never "you sent too many parameters." That's the trap: the API validates combinations, not individual fields, and the error text doesn't say which combination it rejected.

According to recent reports, one more detail worth knowing: from and to are in seconds, but the timestamps inside the returned candle objects are also in seconds. Mixing in milliseconds (easy to do if you're used to other exchanges) silently produces empty arrays or absurd ranges rather than an error.

In a recent development, the fix is to pick one paging axis and stick to it. from+limit is the most robust because it's forward-only: you always ask for "the next N candles starting at timestamp T," and you advance T using the data you got back.

The rule: next page's from = last candle's timestamp + interval seconds. Not +1 second in general — +1 only works for the 1s interval. For 1m it's +60, for 1h it's +3600. If you use the interval length, you never re-request the boundary candle and you never skip one.

A few things this loop gets right that naive versions don't:.

Industry observers note that the 10,000-point cap is per call, not per range, and it's applied to the most recent data in the window you asked for. This has a nasty consequence: if you request from = now - 30 days with limit = 1000 on 1m, you get the 1,000 most recent minutes of that window — not the first 1,000 minutes. Your pagination loop's first page is fine, but the semantics of "most recent within the window" mean that a naive loop which advances from will eventually get stuck asking for data older than what the server will serve in a single call.

Industry observers note that the clean way to handle it is to split the overall range into windows of at most 10,000 intervals, and paginate inside each window. That way each from+limit call is guaranteed to fall inside the server's per-call ceiling.

If you're pulling months of 1m data, this is dozens of HTTP round-trips. That's expected — there is no bulk export endpoint, and hammering the server with parallel requests will get you rate-limited. Serialize, add a small sleep between windows, and cache to disk.

The Gate.io case is one instance of a general problem: undocumented parameter interactions. When you hit a 400 and the message is unhelpful, don't guess — bisect.

The idea: start with a request you know works, then add parameters one at a time, and when it breaks, remove one at a time to confirm which combination is fatal. For a small parameter set this is a few requests.

It has been revealed that for three optional parameters this is at most 8 requests and it tells you definitively that {from, to, limit} is the failing triple and {from, limit} is the maximal working pair. That's far faster than reading docs that don't mention the rule.

Recent findings suggest that when the parameter space is larger — say, ten optional query params — exhaustive subsets are 1,024 requests, which is too many. Switch to a greedy bisection: add params one at a time in the order you suspect matters; when adding one breaks the request, mark it as conflicting with the current set and try it alone against the required params. That's O(n) in practice.

In a recent development, run it, and you get a working parameter set plus the list of params that broke it. In the Gate.io case, rejected would contain whichever of from/to/limit was added third — which is exactly the information the error message withheld.

Recent findings suggest that the general lesson transfers: when an API's parameters interact, the docs often describe each field in isolation and leave the constraints implicit. Build a small probe harness once, and every latest endpoint becomes a five-minute investigation instead of an afternoon of guessing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you've tried to create a private app in HubSpot recently and the option wasn't there, you're not doing anything wrong. HubSpot changed how server-to-server integrations get their credentials, and most tutorials online still describe the old path.

According to recent reports, private apps were the simple way to give a script access to your HubSpot data: create the app, pick scopes, copy a token. That flow is now closed for latest legacy apps. HubSpot's direction is two credential types: project-based apps built with the developer platform, and Service Keys for straightforward data integrations.

For a typical marketing or sales operations script (read deals, read contacts, send events somewhere else), a Service Key covers it.

It's sent like any Bearer token:.

That call is also the fastest way to get the internal IDs of your pipeline stages, which is what your code should compare against (never the stage labels, someone will rename them).

In a recent development, the one real limitation: Service Keys don't support webhooks. Webhooks need a project-based app built with the HubSpot CLI.

Sources indicate that for most integrations, polling is the more robust option anyway. Every few minutes, search for records modified since the last run:.

In a recent development, nothing breaks today. Put two things on the calendar: replace the token with a Service Key, and move your endpoints to the date-versioned paths. Both are small changes if your code keeps the base path and the credential in configuration, not scattered through the script.

Recent findings suggest that A common use for these scripts is closing the loop between HubSpot and Meta Ads: when a deal is qualified or won, an event goes to the Conversions API so campaigns learn which leads actually turn into customers. That's layer 4 of the 4-Layer Tracking Kit, which builds the whole path with a Service Key, the 2026-03 API and polling, including the HubSpot API pitfalls that return status 200 and do nothing.

Do my existing HubSpot private app tokens stop working?

No. Tokens from legacy private apps that already exist keep working. What changed is that existing accounts can no longer create newly introduced legacy private apps. HubSpot has confirmed the end of support for legacy apps and for the v1 to v3 APIs in September 2027, so plan the migration before then.

What replaces private apps for a simple server-to-server script?

A Service Key. You create it in the account settings, give it only the scopes the script needs, and send it as a Bearer token. For a script that reads deals and contacts, read-only CRM scopes are enough.

Can I receive HubSpot webhooks with a Service Key?

No. Webhooks require a project-based app built with the HubSpot CLI. With a Service Key, the robust alternative is polling the search API every few minutes for records modified since the last run.

In a recent development, originally published at https://lp.bitencourtco.com/kit-tracking/en/guides/hubspot-private-apps-service-keys/ by Bitencourt & Co. The full setup, from the ad click to HubSpot deal stages back to Meta, is in the 4-Layer Tracking Kit.

  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, said:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The campaign's spend doesn't change; the number of conversions it reports does.
  • Meta compares events from the pixel and the Conversions API.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You turn on the Conversions API, and a few days later cost per conversion drops by half. It looks like the best week of the account. Usually it isn't: Meta is counting the same conversion twice, once from the browser and once from the server.

The campaign's spend doesn't change; the number of conversions it reports does. Twice the conversions for the same spend means half the cost per conversion. Optimization also starts learning from inflated counts, which is worse than the reporting problem.

Meta compares events from the pixel and the Conversions API. When the event name and the event_id match, it keeps one. In the pixel, the ID goes in the options object:.

Industry observers note that on the server, it goes in the event_id field of the event. With server-side GTM, the GA4 hit carries it from the browser and the Conversions API tag forwards it.

Generate the ID once, where the event is born, and hand the same value to every destination:.

Two rules come with it: one try/catch per destination, so a failure in one doesn't silently stop the others, and no second ID generated in GTM or on the server.

Industry observers note that deduplication is one of 13 silent failure modes covered in the free field guide 13 Silent Tracking Failures. The full setup, from the page to HubSpot deal stages flowing back to Meta, is in the 4-Layer Tracking Kit.

How does Meta deduplicate browser and server events?

When the pixel and the Conversions API send the same event with the same event name and the same event_id, Meta keeps one. In the pixel the ID goes in the eventID option; on the server it goes in the event_id field.

Where should the event_id be created?

Recent findings suggest that once, where the event is born, on the page. The same value goes to the pixel and to the dataLayer, and from there to the server. Generating it twice, in two places, is the same as not having it.

Do CRM events need deduplication?

Not with the browser, because there's no browser counterpart. They still need a stable event_id per record and stage, so a script that runs twice doesn't send the same conversion twice.

According to recent reports, originally published at https://lp.bitencourtco.com/kit-tracking/en/guides/meta-capi-deduplication-event-id/ by Bitencourt & Co. The full setup, from the ad click to HubSpot deal stages back to Meta, is in the 4-Layer Tracking Kit.

Tech Report: 1-Wall Floor Proposal Scale Calibration & Parametric Wall Resizing in Pure TypeScript

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When someone snaps a photo of a hand-drawn floor plan or traces an existing PDF listing sheet, the geometry starts out in arbitrary pixel coordinates.
  • In PlanCaliber, all three operations—1-wall scale calibration, centerline/clear-interior parametric wall resizing, and collinear wall-chain dragging—run deterministically in pure TypeScript with zero external geometry kernels (src/lib/cad/healer.ts).
  • Here is the exact math and edge-case protection behind each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When someone snaps a photo of a hand-drawn floor plan or traces an existing PDF listing sheet, the geometry starts out in arbitrary pixel coordinates. Turning that rough sketch into true-scale architectural inches (1/4" = 1'-0") and then letting the user type exact laser-measure dimensions—without warping walls into trapezoids, stretching a 30-inch range into a 41-inch monster, or folding an adjacent bathroom inside-out—is one of the trickiest UX and geometry problems in browser-based CAD.

In PlanCaliber, all three operations—1-wall scale calibration, centerline/clear-interior parametric wall resizing, and collinear wall-chain dragging—run deterministically in pure TypeScript with zero external geometry kernels (src/lib/cad/healer.ts).

Here is the exact math and edge-case protection behind each one.

After tracing a sketch or PDF, a homeowner or appraiser rarely knows the exact pixel-to-inch scale—they know one real tape-measure reading (for example, "this exterior garage wall is 22'-0"").

Naively multiplying every number in the document by factor = targetLengthIn / curLen breaks physical reality:.

Instead, rescalePlanToWall anchors scaling at the plan's bounding-box origin (ox, oy), scales coordinates uniformly, preserves wall thicknesses and fixed appliance sizes, and snaps architectural openings to 2" rough increments and modular cabinets to 3" stock increments:.

Why anchor around (ox, oy) rather than (0, 0)? Because scaling around the world origin flings the floor plan off-screen if the user panned away from (0, 0) before calibrating. Anchoring to the plan's minimum corner keeps the drawing planted right in the viewport.

Recent findings suggest that when a contractor reads a blueprint, walls are typically dimensioned centerline-to-centerline or exterior face-to-face. When a homeowner measures a room with a laser tape measure, they measure clear interior drywall-to-drywall.

If a user types 12'-0" (144") in clear mode on a bedroom wall framed between a 6" exterior wall and a 4.5" interior partition, the true CAD centerline span is not 144"—it is:.

144" + (6" / 2) + (4.5" / 2) = 149.25" (12'-5 1/4").

setWallLength inspects every perpendicular wall (|dir · od| < 0.25) attached to either endpoint and accumulates half of each intersecting wall's thickness:.

Moving just wall.endId along (dirX, dirY) turns a rectangle into a trapezoid. Even worse: if a bedroom sits next to a 4'-0" hallway and the user widens the bedroom by +5'-0", shifting only the shared partition wall pushes it past the far hallway wall, inverting the hallway polygon into a negative-area self-intersecting bowtie.

PlanCaliber solves both in two clean graph passes:.

Right after applying dirX * delta and dirY * delta, every door and window on a stretched or shrunk wall updates its offset proportionally ((op.offsetIn / oldL) * newL) and runs through clampOpeningsInPlace so no jamb ever overlaps a corner (>= 3" minimum return).

Industry observers note that in a real planar floor-plan graph, interior partition T-junctions split a 48'-0" exterior south wall into three separate segments (say 16'-0", 14'-0", and 18'-0"). If the user grabs the middle segment to deepen the whole house by 2'-0", dragging only that single segment punches a jagged step into the exterior envelope.

collectCollinearWallChainVertices computes the seed wall's unit normal (nx, ny) = (-dy/len, dx/len) and floods across connected same-kind (exterior or interior) segments whose endpoints lie within 0.5" of the line and whose direction dot-product with the normal is <= 0.02:.

Restricting the flood by w.kind === seed.kind is essential: an interior partition that happens to align with a jogged exterior wall stays independent unless the user edits it explicitly.

You can test the full workflow right in the browser with no account required:.

Note: PlanCaliber exports are preliminary architectural space-planning and drafting documents; field-verify all measurements on site and consult a licensed architect or structural engineer where permits require stamped drawings.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

It has been revealed that figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically key—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing challenges when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Sources indicate that figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model indicates, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

Recent findings suggest that to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

It has been revealed that after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

According to recent reports, we use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

Recent findings suggest that in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient update therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Sources indicate that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

Industry observers note that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

It has been revealed that figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Industry observers note that figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

It has been revealed that we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

According to recent reports, granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that short answer: an AI-built landing page can look finished in the preview and still fail on speed: an oversized hero image delaying the main content, elements that jump as fonts and images load, and scripts that make taps feel slow.
  • The gain is small and concrete: a page you can hand to a client or ship without a "why is it slow on my phone?" follow-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, disclosure: I work on VibUI, a paid catalogue of website prompts. It appears once, near the end. The review below needs only a browser and whichever AI tool you already use.

Industry observers note that short answer: an AI-built landing page can look finished in the preview and still fail on speed: an oversized hero image delaying the main content, elements that jump as fonts and images load, and scripts that make taps feel slow. Spend fifteen minutes on three metrics (Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift and Interaction to Next Paint), write each finding back into the prompt as a constraint, and regenerate only the section that failed. This applies to output from v0, Lovable, Bolt, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Replit, GitHub Copilot, Framer AI, Google Stitch, Readdy, Aura.build and OpenAI Codex.

The gain is small and concrete: a page you can hand to a client or ship without a "why is it slow on my phone?" follow-up. It is not a promise of any ranking or conversion change.

In a recent development, A preview demonstrates a fast laptop on a good connection. The problems are invisible there:.

Treat these as lab numbers. Real-user (field) data only exists after real visitors arrive, so do not quote a lab score as a result.

In a recent development, ask the tool to list every external request. That one line catches most of the surprise scripts before you open DevTools.

Recent findings suggest that if you build one page a quarter, keep the block above in a snippets file and skip any paid library. A catalogue earns its place only when you repeat the same section types often and want starting briefs that already carry constraints like these.

In a recent development, if you want to inspect one: The library I work on is VibUI. It has 2,852 website prompt templates (775 full pages, 1,100 sections, 817 components and 160 animated backgrounds), and about 1,000 of them include source code. Payment is one-time with no auto-renewal: $48 quarterly, $99 yearly, or $179 lifetime (listed down from $384). The yearly and lifetime aims also include 2,407 AI video prompts. There are 60 free samples, and a free account can copy 2 prompts. Try a free sample on a real section, run it through the review above, and only consider paying if it saves you setup time on pages you will actually build.

Is a perfect Lighthouse score the goal?

Industry observers note that no. Use it to find the largest problems. A page that scores a little lower but loads its main content quickly on a phone is better than one tuned to the test.

Not necessarily. Keep it cheap (CSS transforms and opacity), keep it away from the first screen, and respect reduced-motion settings.

Can the AI tool fix these issues by itself?

Industry observers note that it can, if you hand it the specific finding ("LCP element is the hero image, no dimensions") and ask it to change only that section. Vague requests like "make it faster" rarely help.

Do I need to pay for a library to follow this review?

Recent findings suggest that no. Everything above works with free tools and the AI builder you already use.
