💡 Key Takeaways
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a latest attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, showed a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also indicated a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

#218170. An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning

An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Chrhenning

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so.
  • Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.
  • Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful.

Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.

Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show.

Industry observers note that in my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong.This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis .

Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes indicates how plausible each one is, given what we know.

It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty:.

It has been revealed that the line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have.Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure.

A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters.

It has been revealed that all of these need the uncertainty to be useful. To see when it is, it makes sense to look at where it comes from.

As a running example, we look at steering angle prediction. The input is the image from a car’s front camera, and the output $y$ is the steering angle. Such datasets can be recorded cheaply from human drivers. Take a car approaching a point where the road splits. In the left lane, drivers mostly go left. In the right lane, they mostly go right. In the middle lane, which points straight at the divider, about half go left and half go right.

According to recent reports, the car’s position across the lanes is implicit in the camera image. To keep the figures simple, we use it directly as a one-dimensional input $x$ in the figures below.The rest of the image, such as where the road goes, matters just as much for the prediction. We implicitly assume that the model knows it, since it cannot be compressed into a simple one-dimensional variable that keeps the explanations easy to follow.

What we want to learn is the conditional distribution $p^*(y \mid x)$: for each position, how likely each steering angle is. As is common in statistical learning theory, we assume that the data come from a fixed joint distribution $p^*(x, y)$, and the recordings from human drivers are samples from it.

Sources indicate that the ground truth $p^*(y \mid x)$ is just one of many possible conditional distributions.Strictly speaking, the truth is only defined where $p^*(x) > 0$. Many hypotheses agree with it on the road but differ off the road, where no data can tell them apart. We call each conditional distribution of $y$ given $x$ a hypothesis, and together they form a space. As we will see, learning amounts to searching a subset of this space.

That subset is the model, a family of hypotheses indexed by parameters $\theta$. A common choice for regression is a Gaussian whose mean is a neural network $f_\theta(x)$ and whose variance $\sigma^2$ is fixed:.

According to recent reports, the truth need not lie inside the model. For the lane split, it does not: a single Gaussian has one peak, but in the middle lane the truth has two.

Training picks the hypothesis that best explains the data. It minimizes the negative log-likelihood (NLL), the average of $-\log p_\theta(y_i \mid x_i)$ over the training examples. For the Gaussian with fixed variance, this is the familiar mean squared errorI walked through this connection, from the KL divergence to the mean squared error, in an earlier post.:.

So a network trained with mean squared error already has an uncertainty model, even if nobody chose it on purpose.

According to recent reports, how far is the trained model from the truth? The expected NLL splits into two terms:.

In a recent development, where both expectations are over the true data distribution. The first term is the KL divergence, which measures how far the model is from the truth and is zero only if they match. The second is the entropy of the truth, its aleatoric uncertainty, which does not depend on the model. Minimizing the NLL therefore moves the model toward the truth. But we never know the entropy of the truth, so the NLL alone cannot tell us how far away we still are.This is why we are usually blind to model misspecification: a low NLL does not tell us whether the truth lies inside the model. I will get back to this later. Moreover, even the KL divergence would not be enough, since it is an average over all inputs. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so a model can be close to the truth on average and still steer into the divider. Knowing which inputs matter takes domain expertise, which is ultimately the modeller's responsibility.

It has been revealed that back in the middle lane, the single peak has a dangerous consequence. The mean squared error is minimized by the average steering angle, and the average of left and right is straight ahead, into the divider. No choice of parameters avoids this, because every hypothesis in the model has a single peak. In an earlier post, I looked at this example in more detail, and we studied it in a paper on misspecification, the case where the truth lies outside the model .

The fix is a model that contains the truth. For this example, a mixture of two Gaussians, whose weights, means and variances are all outputs of the network, is enough to contain the truth.

Sources indicate that understanding the problem well enough to make this choice is the modeller’s job. But a richer model is not free: it contains more hypotheses, so the data has to do more work to single out the right one.This is the familiar bias–variance tradeoff. For example, a fully connected network can represent everything a convolutional network can. Yet for images we use convolutional networks, because they leave out hypotheses that do not fit images and so need much less data. Their assumptions seem stronger than necessary, though: with enough data, vision transformers, which assume less, do better.

It has been revealed that since the mixture contains the truth, enough data brings it close, including in the middle lane. Only then is its spread the aleatoric uncertainty: with the given information, even a perfect model cannot say which lane a particular driver will take.As with the coin flip, what counts as aleatoric depends on what the input contains. If $x$ were random noise, it would carry no information, and the best fit would ignore it and learn the distribution of steering angles independent of the input, $p(y)$. A rear camera image is more deceptive. Steering changes slowly (it is strongly autocorrelated), so the view behind the car shows how the driver steered a moment ago, and repeating that is usually a good guess. The validation error decreases as expected during training, yet the model can never anticipate a turn, because the road ahead is not in the input. I discuss this gap between predicting and forecasting in an earlier post.

In a recent development, but in practice we do not know the truth, so we cannot check the fit like this. How do we know how much we still do not know?

Industry observers note that so far, training gave us a single hypothesis. But with only 20 data points, many hypotheses explain the data about equally well, and by picking one of them, we ignore that the data cannot tell them apart. Bayesian inference instead keeps all of them.Bayesian inference is not the only way to capture epistemic uncertainty, but it is a principled one, and the one I know best.

Before seeing any data, we decide how plausible each hypothesis in the model is. This is the prior $p(\theta)$, a soft inductive bias. It captures what we know, or assume, before training, and everything the model does not know is measured relative to it.Choosing a prior can feel arbitrary, and often it is. Think of a CNN, which rules out hypotheses that do not suit images. A prior does not rule them out, but it makes them less plausible from the start. I discuss how the prior shapes what a model does not know in an earlier post. Data then shifts the weight to the hypotheses that explain it, giving rise to the posterior:.

According to recent reports, where $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ is the data. The likelihood, written $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)$ for short, measures how well hypothesis $\theta$ agrees with the data.

To predict, we average all hypotheses, each weighted by its posterior probability. This is the posterior predictive:.

With more and more data, the posterior concentrates on a single hypothesis: the one in the model that is closest to the truth.Closest in KL divergence. This holds under regularity conditions, including that the prior puts enough weight near that hypothesis . If the model contains the truth, that hypothesis is the truth itself. If not, as in the sketch below, it is only the best the model has to offer.

This picture splits uncertainty into three sources, using the terms of Hüllermeier and Waegeman . What sets them apart is what reduces them:.

According to recent reports, the last point matters in practice. A misspecified model can still have a confident posterior: it is confident about the least wrong hypothesis it contains.

According to recent reports, both models above show more uncertainty where data is missing. That is approximation uncertainty, and both capture it. To also question the model itself, a full probabilistic treatment would weigh models too, but that is hard in practice. What we can do is compare a few candidate models. For this, Bayesian inference offers the evidence, $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathcal{M}) = \int p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{M}) \, \mathrm{d}\theta$, the probability of the data under model $\mathcal{M}$, averaged over its prior.The notation can be misleading, since it suggests that we treat the model as a random variable. We do not have to, so a semicolon, $p(\mathcal{D}; \mathcal{M})$, might be a preferable notation. Note also that $\mathcal{M}$ now includes the prior: the same hypotheses with a different prior form a different model. Here it clearly prefers the mixture.The evidence has a built-in Occam's razor : a more flexible model spreads its prior over more possible datasets, so it pays a price unless the data need that flexibility. Here, the two lanes do. But it only ranks the models we try, and if none of them contains the truth, it will not tell us.

In a recent development, like the KL divergence earlier, the evidence is an average over all data. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so their effect can vanish in the evidence, and the simpler model may even win. Domain knowledge would tell us otherwise. This is why choosing the model remains the modeller’s job, and comparing models is a tool for it, not a replacement.

Sources indicate that so far, we have taken the prior as given. But the prior is part of the model. In theory, with enough data, its choice stops mattering, as long as it does not rule out the right hypotheses. In practice, we rarely have that much data, and a poor prior, like any poor inductive bias, can hurt a lot. I discussed this in more detail in earlier posts on uncertainty and on continual learning.

Industry observers note that in short, the posterior is uncertain where the data and our assumptions leave room for disagreement. Low uncertainty therefore does not mean we have seen data there. Generalization works exactly this way: far from the data, the inductive bias makes the hypotheses agree. If the bias is good, the model is confident and right. If not, it is confident and wrong.

Sometimes we want a statistical guarantee, ideally one that does not depend on our modelling choices, since those can be arbitrarily wrong. Conformal prediction gives such a guarantee. Instead of a single prediction, it outputs a prediction set that contains the true output, say, 90% of the time. This is called 90% coverage. It wraps any trained model, and as long as the data are exchangeable, the guarantee holds no matter how wrong the model is .

According to recent reports, conformal prediction comes in many flavors. We look at the simplest and most common one, split conformal prediction. Its recipe has four steps:.

If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the set has at least 90% coverage. This holds on average over inputs, not for any particular input, such as one at the lane split.

But the guarantee does not say whether the sets are useful. For that, we want low scores in the histogram above, since a small $\hat q$ gives tight sets. A poor model has higher scores and gets wider sets, with the same coverage.

The guarantee only needs a calibration set. Useful sets also need the same modelling work as before. I wrote more about this in a recent post on conformal prediction.

So far, the goal was a faithful uncertainty: a predictive distribution close to the truth. But uncertainty is meant to be used, and decision theory claims how. The model provides a belief $p(y \mid x)$. Whoever acts provides a loss $L(a, y)$, the cost of action $a$ if the outcome turns out to be $y$. We then pick the action with the lowest expected loss:.

According to recent reports, in the lane split, the action is a steering angle. The belief claims which angles drivers take: left or right, never straight. The loss says what we want. If our destination is to the left, steering left has a low loss, steering right a higher one, and steering into the divider is worst of all. Under the true belief, the decision follows the left lane. A belief with a single peak in the middle rules out neither lane and picks straight.

How faithful does the belief need to be? It depends on the decision.Since the belief is approximate anyway, we can fit it with the loss in mind, so that it is useful for the decision . In the rest of this section, we walk through two practical examples, visual quality inspection and holding reserve for wind power, where the answers differ.

According to recent reports, many factories use cameras to check every part that comes off the line. Mistakes are costly here, since a missed defect may reach a customer, lead to a recall or, in the worst case, put people at risk. To keep things simple, we consider a binary classifier in this section.In practice, a yes or no is rarely enough. We may also want to know where the defect is, its outline, which component it affects and why the model flagged it. It takes the camera image $x$ and outputs the probability $p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ that the part is defective. With stakes this high, should this probability not be faithful, or even come with a guarantee?

To answer this, we look at how the probability turns into a decision. We reject a part if $p = p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ is above a threshold. If we reject, we pay a cost $c_{FP}$ when the part is good, which happens with probability $1 - p$. If we ship, we pay a cost $c_{FN}$ when it is defective, which happens with probability $p$. Rejecting is cheaper on average when $c_{FP}\,(1 - p) < c_{FN}\,p$, that is, when.

Sources indicate that what this derivation hides is that it takes $p$ at face value, so it assumes the model is calibrated: of all parts scored 0.1, about 10% should be defective. In this example, though, calibration matters less than it seems, for two reasons. First, calibrated against whom? Inspectors disagree on borderline parts, and since labels are expensive, each part is usually labeled by only one of them. So the labels can only tell us whether the model is calibrated against whoever labeled the data, and on borderline parts, another inspector would have labeled differently. Second, $c_{FN}$ includes recalls, lost customers and reputation, so it is rarely known. It is not even a single number, since a customer may never notice a faint scratch, while a deep crack can make the part fail. So the threshold is a guess anyway.

In a recent development, what about a guarantee, such as “at most 5% of defects escape”? The guarantee we got from conformal prediction earlier does not give this. It holds on average over all parts, and since defects are rare, it can be met while missing most of them. We need coverage for defects alone. Conformal prediction can give this too, if we set the threshold using defects only. Then at most a fraction $\alpha$ of defects, here 5%, score below it .

In a recent development, this guarantee has a price. Labeled defects are rare and expensive to collect, and we need many of them for a stable threshold. Worse, a defect is anything that is not normal. The guarantee holds only for defects that are exchangeable with the ones we collected, and the next one may look like none of them.Indeed, defects are so rare that practical solutions often teach the model with defect-free images only, an approach I worked on at Ethon (see here and here). Finally, the guarantee fixes the threshold, however many good parts it rejects.

If the model rejects too many good parts and we raise the threshold, we give up the guarantee and are back to costs we cannot measure.

It has been revealed that so in this example, we need neither calibration nor a guarantee. Since $c_{FN}$ is unknown, an operator tunes the threshold by hand, and for that, only the order of the scores matters: they should grow with the severity of a flaw. Small scratches are rarely called defects and deep cracks almost always, and in between, inspectors disagree. A model calibrated against a large pool of inspectors would give such a score, but these labels are too expensive. Getting the order right without them is hard modelling work: we have to build the right inductive biases into the model, for instance during pre-training.

Wind power depends on the weather, so a grid operator never knows exactly how much will arrive. To cover a shortfall, meaning less wind power than planned, the operator keeps backup power on standby, called the reserve. Unlike inspecting parts, no person could forecast the shortfall by hand, so the model learns it from past data alone. It takes inputs $x$, such as the weather forecast and recent measurements, and outputs a distribution $p(\text{shortfall} \mid x)$ over the shortfall. If the shortfall exceeds the reserve, we have a shortage, and each missing unit costs $c_{\text{short}}$, and each unit of reserve that goes unused costs $c_{\text{idle}}$.In practice, $c_{\text{short}}$ is much larger. A shortage must be covered within minutes, by fast and expensive plants, by buying power at short notice or, in the worst case, by cutting off customers. Idle reserve only costs what it takes to keep a plant ready. Unlike $c_{FN}$ in visual inspection, both costs can be roughly estimated, for instance from market prices, so for the sake of argument, we take them as known.

The best reserve is the $\tau$-quantile of the predicted shortfall, with.

In a recent development, the costs pick the quantile.Why the $\tau$-quantile? Say we hold a reserve $r$ and add one more unit. If the shortfall turns out larger than $r$, the unit is used and saves $c_{\text{short}}$. Otherwise, it sits idle and costs $c_{\text{idle}}$. So the unit pays off when $c_{\text{short}}\, P(\text{shortfall} > r) > c_{\text{idle}}\, P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$. As $r$ grows, the left side shrinks and the right side grows, so we add reserve until both are equal. With $P(\text{shortfall} > r) = 1 - P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$, this gives $P(\text{shortfall} \le r) = \tau$, which is the $\tau$-quantile. Since these costs change by the hour, so does $\tau$.

It has been revealed that to see what this asks of the model, we again take a Gaussian model for simplicity. On most days, the forecast is roughly right, and the shortfall is small. But on rare days, the wind dies down unexpectedly, and the shortfall is large. So in the tail, the truth is not Gaussian. Since shortages are costly, $\tau$ is high, and the reserve sits far out in the tail of the predicted distribution, so the model has to get these rare, large shortfalls right.

It has been revealed that if we proposal for a shortage 1 in 10 times ($\tau = 90\%$), the two dots almost coincide, and the Gaussian works well. Now say we plan for 1 in 100 ($\tau = 99\%$). The Gaussian sets the reserve at the blue dot. But how often this reserve falls short is decided by the truth, and at this reserve, the orange curve lies well above 1 in 100. Shortages come more than twice as often as planned. Unlike in visual inspection, the probabilities are used at face value here,Why not adjust the reserve by hand, as the operator did with the threshold? In inspection, there is one threshold to tune. Here, $\tau$ changes by the hour, so every quantile would need tuning, and shortages are too rare to notice when one is off. and since $\tau$ changes by the hour, the whole distribution must be faithful, tail included.

It has been revealed that in a year of daily data, a 1-in-100 shortfall highlights up only a few times, and anything rarer than once a year not at all. So where we need the uncertainty most, in the tail, we have the least data, and the assumptions built into the model decide the answer. We have to choose them from what we know about wind and weather.

Recent findings suggest that every model in this post made an assumption about uncertainty, whether we chose it or not. Making it faithful took real work: a likelihood that can represent the truth, enough data to find it, and inductive biases that hold up where the data runs out.

That work is not always needed. Our own uncertainty is not faithful either. We humans misjudge probabilities in well-known ways , yet we handle most everyday tasks just fine. In this post, too, we saw tasks where uncertainty did not have to be faithful, and others where it counted. So before investing in faithful uncertainty, ask what you gain from it. And even when it does not have to be faithful, I believe it helps to know what faithful would mean. Then we know what our uncertainty gets wrong and can judge whether that matters for the decision.

Feedback is welcome. If you think this introduction misses an key aspect, or you know other examples where making uncertainty useful matters, please leave a comment below.

#218167. Breaking: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lia ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lia

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture.
  • The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page.
  • Sources indicate that there is a better way to measure culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that claims about either of us.

The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the tech giant calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.

Sources indicate that there is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.

Recent findings suggest that take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.

The square root is crucial. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a tech giant of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.

We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.

The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.

To account for this, we also measure the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).

Industry observers note that if P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.

Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.

For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:.

Industry observers note that as with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the manufacturer logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.

It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of owners, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.

If your tech giant uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.

If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.

It has been revealed that culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

13 Sam's Club Bakery Items, Ranked Worst To Best

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery.
  • In a recent development, to get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past.
  • It has been revealed that the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery. The full-service department offers everything from sliced bread and rolls for everyday use to custom cakes for your most special occasions. Like the other items under the warehouse roof, the bakery stocks bulk quantities and super-sized versions of many of its best-loved bakes, giving your bank account a bit of a breather without requiring you to give up your appetite for the good stuff.

In a recent development, to get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past. I scooped up a selection of breads, rolls, and sugary delights to put under the microscope — my taste buds — and see how they rank amongst one another. Simple items like plain bagels shared the table with deluxe creations like caramel pecan banana loaf, all purchased at my Phoenix, Arizona-area Sam's locations. Prices and products shown are likely to vary based on region and warehouse. Clearly, membership has its privileges, but they're not all equally worth your money or your attention.

It has been revealed that the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf. It's crusty and tender, perfect for breaking off chunks and dipping into olive oil or cheese dip. But it does limit your uses to silver dollar-sized slices, making mini garlic toast or bruschetta the most likely purposes. Slicing it lengthwise in longer sections will extend your toasting potential, but it's still a lot of bread to blow through before it starts to get even crustier on the counter.

Unless you have a house load of diners to feed, you may be getting more bread than you need, in a size and shape that makes using leftovers a bit limited. So while the bread itself is a wonderful version of a bakery-style baguette, the drawbacks of having two super-skinny loaves to work through may be reason enough to make a more suitable choice than this grocery store French bread.

Recent findings suggest that there's no sense in raving over how good a plain bagel can be. They're plain for a reason: so they can hold all kinds of spreads and shmears and fillings without the taste of ramped-up bread getting in the way. But that doesn't mean every bakery gets the basic formula for plain bagels right. So having a bodacious bag of six overly large, unadorned bagels waiting at Sam's Club, among the fancier flavors, is a comfort to the purists of the bread-loving world. They do make an attractive haul at only $3.82 for six large pre-cut bagels, so there's that, at least.

Recent findings suggest that I'm a fan of bagels, largely for the dense chewiness they offer, similar to a pretzel but with more potential for add-ons that don't fall off. I'd love to endorse these bagels more heartily, since they do their job perfectly well at a price that doesn't feel like you're being gouged. But in the end, they're just bagels, and Sam's has so many preferable baked goods waiting to be tossed in your cart.

Sam's Club is famous for its generous 12-inch pumpkin pies that appear at holiday time, priced at a seasonally considerate $5.98. But beyond the size and price, the warehouse bakery doesn't do much out of the ordinary with this bake. The crust is standard, the filling is customary, and the experience of digging into a slice is perfectly passable. In fact, if you're a dessert traditionalist, this will do nicely to replace anything you were planning on making yourself.

But the fact that the company mass-produces its pumpkin pies every year means you know exactly what you're getting here. If you keep your expectations in check and top it with a drizzle of chocolate or caramel sauce, plus some king-sized dollops of whipped cream, you can make it through another serving this year. Just don't count on it being anything more than average, even under all the decorations. You might even fare a little better with the comparable-yet-superior Costco pumpkin pie this year instead.

Something about the recipe Sam's Club bakery uses for its yeast dinner rolls makes them better than the thaw-and-bake versions I've become accustomed to. The chewy crust and soft centers of these baked spheres make them far too easy to snack on, which could readily deplete your stock for actual meals. The oversized bag comes with 24 rolls, so maybe you'll have enough for both if you can keep your appetite for bread snacks under control.

According to recent reports, maybe the best thing about these rolls is the price. You can drop $3.98 and end up with more bread than you can shake a stick at — a true magic trick in an economy that seems intent on crushing shoppers just hoping to come home with the basics. It'll put your imagination to the test when you realize your leftovers are crying out for creativity — cream puffs, mini-sandwiches, and bread pudding are all possibilities. Even if you freeze what you don't use for meals down the line, you'll be glad you made the purchase.

Sources indicate that similar to the yeast dinner rolls, Sam's Club bakery's brioche slider rolls are three-bite beauties that come pre-sliced to be filled with your favorite accouterments. But whether you opt to use them as dinner rolls or just toast them up and spread a little peanut butter inside instead of making actual sliders, they'll be just as satisfying. They have a buttery, eggy flavor that mimics full-sized brioche buns; the only thing reduced here is the scale, and even that makes them a fun choice for kid-size sandwiches of all sorts.

In a recent development, for $6.98, you get a generous stash of 24 slider buns. That may seem like too many, but if you use them in place of sliced bread for school lunches and work them into weekend meals, you'll blow through a whole bag before you know it. And if they're among your DIY barbecue spread or holiday celebration as cold cut holders, your guests are sure to gush over how cute and delicious they are.

Tangy, chewy, and ready to eat right out of the bag, the sliced sourdough loaves from Sam's Club bakery are a fantastic alternative to the rectangular bagged loaves the warehouse sells in its commercial bread aisle. It's the sort of sturdy bread that holds up well as grilled cheese sandwiches, Reubens without rye, and French toast, though you'll need to cut the slices in half for easier handling. And you can certainly cut it into strips to add to your grazing board for get-togethers or brunch sessions. It's the every-bread, and it's only $3.96 a loaf.

I tried to think of some drawbacks for this accommodating bake, but came up short. Despite having a host of sugary bites on the list that knocked my socks off, I thought this sourdough was excellent. It's pushed aside my usual go-to seedy whole-grain loaves to become my preferred full-size bread and an every-visit purchase.

Cocktail croissants, as Sam's Club calls them, are the bakery's sensibly sized version of the French classic, given all the love and attention of their continental counterparts, even in a warehouse grocery department setting. There's flakiness galore, thanks to an all-butter recipe that also comes through in the rich flavor. A carton of 20 croissants priced at $5.98, yet made with the same quality as their boulangerie counterparts, could be the bargain of our lifetimes.

The size is perfect for snacking, much better than the larger, sandwich-friendly croissants that cry out for fillings. Sure, you can break a bigger croissant into smaller pieces to make noshing a little more restrained. But when you can complete one in a few bites and walk away? That's sensibly sized croissant business. And if you're a fan of French pastries but cringe at spending big money to enjoy them, this first-rate batch of happiness is your golden opportunity, no splurging necessary.

Now this savage bake looks like the Ferrari of Sam's Club offerings, even before you take it out of the box. Through the cellophane window on top, you can see a heart-stopping coating of crumble in the perfect shade of toasted brown. The split in the top reveals a peek of golden pound cake. The overall effect is that you've stumbled onto the most gourmet banana bread you've ever encountered — right across from the bulk fabric softener and double-paned window vendors.

In a recent development, the chewy crust is just shy of decadence, feeling more like an old-fashioned homemade crumble top without the oats. The banana bread beneath is equal parts sweet loaf and pound cake, capturing the cozy vibe but with a stroke of elegance that elevates it. I would eat this in all forms: cold out of the freezer, room temperature straight out of the box, or warmed up with a scoop of ice cream on the side. There's no situation that this fantastic loaf can't handle.

Sources indicate that gourmet bakeries have nothing on the patisserie spirit of Sam's Club mini creme pies. These refrigerated bakes shrink the lush goodness of full-sized pies into a six-pack of petite pastries, two each of chocolate creme, peanut butter chocolate, and cherry cheese pie. The reduced scale doesn't diminish the delicious returns; there's bold flavor and silky texture that make even a single slice a luxurious moment.

Though all of these pies are a real treat, there's a definite hierarchy to their enjoyability. The cherry cheese pie is a mellow bite that resurrects the vintage pie flavor from long-ago Sunday dinner desserts, while the chocolate creme reminds me of a dessert-style specialty. But the top spot belongs to the peanut butter chocolate pie, which calls to mind luxury cheesecakes made by maestros of the baking world. It's a sweet dream of a Sam's Club baked goodie, and at $10.98 for six, it's one that doesn't require reservations — of any kind.

Recent findings suggest that any Sam's Club shopper will tell you that the bakery muffins are a cake situation, not a muffin scenario. These super-sweet, super-sized bakes are too massive and too delicious to qualify as traditional muffins, and when the warehouse puts a holiday spin on the usual recipes, that dessert-ready razzmatazz doubles up. They're the domed bakery-style muffins too, so they look extra grand on your snacking spread.

In a recent development, I've had the store's traditional chocolate, blueberry, and banana nut muffins enough to be inured to their charms by now. But slicing into these three upgraded flavors was a seasonal revelation I won't soon get over. The red velvet is the best of the bunch, tasting like a pricey chef-inspired creation, while the pumpkin spice takes a more measured approach than the usual fall-flavored treats. And the butter pecan is a study in subtlety, with just the right balance of sweet and earthy notes. These should be year-round items.

It has been revealed that another refrigerated item due to the meltable toppings and delicate frosting, the gourmet cupcake eight-pack at Sam's Club bakery is a fancier take on the workaday cupcakes that come in a set of 30, and all taste exactly the same. In this package, you get a variety of chocolate, strawberry, and Meyer lemon, all wearing the frills and finery you'd find in a much pricier cupcake at a specialty shop. The $12.97 price tag that splits into $1.62 per cake assures you that you can have nice things without having to cash in your IRA.

Even if you choose to crack open your piggy bank for these, you'll be getting more than your money's worth. The chocolate cupcake is exceptional, lush, and over-packed with fudgy goodness thanks to a generous heap of ganache frosting. The strawberry is well-balanced, with its own floral ganache whip, and the Meyer lemon, with a dollop of gelee in the center, is bright as sunshine, authentic-tasting. There's a moist crumb and silky frosting in every cake, too. They're a little too complex to pass off as a home bake, but these are top-tier bakes that make a perfect meal finisher at a dinner party or a lovely surprise for birthday revelers.

I'm a frequent Sam's Club shopper, so I had some idea of which items I thought would be worth including. But with items changing so often and seasonal picks popping up throughout the year, I also grabbed some new selections to give my list a bit of variety. Even familiar items like bagels and baguettes took on a different status when compared to novelties like specialty banana bread and gourmet brownies.

In a recent development, to taste test everything fairly, I used my standard method: the one-bite sample. I gauged freshness and texture as well as taste to arrive at an all-encompassing enjoyability factor for each item. Anything that was deemed worthy of a second or third bite became an obvious high-ranking find, while the items that were less captivating sank to the bottom. The standard-issue picks that were neither dazzling nor disappointing fell somewhere in the middle of the list.

What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

📖 0% read

  • Industry observers note that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years.
  • According to recent reports, if you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Industry observers note that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years. Or maybe you came across it online while searching for ways to cope with a memory that still feels heavy. Whether you’ve heard of EMDR but don’t know how it works, or you’re familiar with the approach but skeptical, we’re here to break it all down.

According to recent reports, if you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes. But the research tells a more reassuring story. It’s a well-studied therapy for trauma, and it’s increasingly explored for anxiety and depression, too.

Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research reveals, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a structured therapy that helps the brain reprocess distressing memories so they carry less emotional weight. Psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, developed it in the late 1980s after she noticed that certain eye movements seemed to ease her own troubling thoughts.

EMDR rests on Shapiro’s adaptive information processing model. The idea is that your brain normally files an experience away, so you can recall it later without feeling like you’re living it again. But a frightening or painful event can interrupt that process, leaving the memory raw and unfiled, still carrying the fear and detail of that moment. That’s why it can resurface later, as vivid as the day it happened.

According to this model, “processing” a memory means helping your brain finish the filing. You don’t forget what happened, and the facts don’t change. What changes is the emotional charge it carries, so recalling it feels less like reliving it and more like remembering it. To help that happen, EMDR uses a technique called “bilateral stimulation.”.

EMDR uses a technique called bilateral stimulation. While you hold a difficult memory in mind, a trained therapist guides you through side-to-side stimulation.

Bilateral stimulation can take a few forms:.

eye movements that follow your therapist’s fingers.

gentle taps that switch between your hands or knees.

tones that play in one ear, then the other.

Sources indicate that there’s a theory behind the side-to-side part, though researchers are still working out exactly why it helps. The leading explanation is about mental bandwidth. Your working memory, the part of your mind that holds what you’re focused on right now, can only handle so much at once. When you track side-to-side movement while recalling a hard memory, the two tasks compete for that limited space. The hard memory tends to feel a little less vivid, and with repetition it can lose its sharp edges, so it feels less overwhelming to hold.

💙 Learn more in our guide to bilateral stimulation.

EMDR has eight phases, though they tend to blend together in practice. The early phases cover your history and teach you coping skills, so you feel prepared before any hard memories arise. In the middle phases, you focus on a specific memory while following bilateral stimulation, which is meant to help your brain reprocess it. The final phases check that the memory feels less distressing and help you close out the work safely.

Industry observers note that the evidence is strong for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a condition that can develop after a frightening or life-threatening event. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of research on a topic) found that EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) both reduce PTSD symptoms. They also outperformed other therapies when researchers checked in after treatment ended. A 2024 review in the Journal of Traumatic Stress identified more than 30 randomized controlled trials supporting EMDR for PTSD in adults and children. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, recommend EMDR for PTSD.

However, some guidelines, including those from the American Psychological Association (APA), rate the evidence for EMDR as less certain than for trauma-focused CBT. Researchers also debate exactly why EMDR works.

💙 Read more about how EMDR can help you cope with PTSD.

Industry observers note that the picture is more mixed outside PTSD. Early research suggests EMDR may help with anxiety, as one meta-analysis found reduced symptoms of anxiety, panic, and phobia, though the studies were small and varied in quality.

Evidence for depression is emerging as well. Another meta-analysis demonstrated reduced depression symptoms, with the strongest effects in more severe cases. These findings are promising, but they don’t carry the same weight as the PTSD research.

It has been revealed that after you and a therapist finish the early phases, you bring a specific memory to mind and notice the thoughts and body sensations that come with it. Then your therapist guides you through the bilateral stimulation while you let your mind go where it goes. You can ask to pause or stop at any time. Unlike many talk therapies, EMDR doesn’t require you to describe the memory in detail.

In a recent development, sessions usually run 60–90 minutes. Your therapist pauses often to check in on what you noticed. Over several rounds of bilateral stimulation, many people find the memory feels less sharp, even though the facts don’t change. Between sessions, a mindfulness practice, such as slow breathing or a body scan, can help you ease feelings that surface.

It draws on the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR, though audio-only versions haven’t been studied on their own the way clinical EMDR has. Think of it as a calming complement to therapy, not a replacement for a trained therapist.

The answer varies, since it depends on what you’re working through. For a single, recent trauma, some people notice their symptoms ease within a handful of sessions. More complex or long-standing trauma usually takes longer, sometimes many months. Therapists describe a typical course as 6–12 sessions, though it varies widely from person to person.

It has been revealed that along the way, some people feel worse before they feel better. Painful memories can stir up strong emotions in the short term, which is common and doesn’t mean EMDR isn’t working. Before reprocessing begins, your therapist teaches you coping skills, such as grounding exercises that anchor you in the present, so you have tools to use if those feelings get intense.

In a recent development, 💙 Try the 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 practice, a quick way to ground yourself in the present, with Prof. Megan Reitz.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a form of therapy that uses bilateral stimulation, such as guided eye movements, to help your brain process distressing memories so they feel less intense. Psychologist Francine Shapiro developed this therapy in the late 1980s.

In a recent development, EMDR may help with anxiety, though PTSD is where the evidence is strongest. The studies on anxiety are smaller and less consistent. If your anxiety is tied to a specific frightening experience, it may be worth asking a therapist whether EMDR fits your situation.

💙 Explore how mindfulness can help you manage your anxiety.

Sources indicate that EMDR differs from talk therapy because it doesn’t require you to describe your experience in detail. You’ll still talk with your therapist, especially early on, but the reprocessing happens while you hold a memory in mind and follow bilateral stimulation. Talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus more on examining and reshaping your thoughts out loud.

The main benefit of EMDR is that it can ease the distress tied to painful memories. For many people with PTSD, that can mean fewer flashbacks and less of that constant, on-alert feeling.

Industry observers note that much of the debate is about why EMDR works, not whether it does. The evidence is strongest for PTSD, with early and more mixed findings for anxiety and depression.

In a recent development, some studies suggest the eye movements themselves add little. The benefit may instead come from giving your mind a second task while you recall a memory, which can make it feel less vivid and emotionally intense. Other tasks that split your attention may have the same effect.

Certain guidelines, including the APA’s, consider the evidence for EMDR less established than for trauma-focused CBT. None of this takes away from the relief many people find with EMDR. It’s useful context as you weigh your options with a therapist.

EMDR is generally safe when a trained therapist delivers it, though you may experience some short-term effects. You might feel more emotional or tired between sessions, or have vivid dreams as your brain keeps processing the memory.

These reactions usually pass within a day or two. If they last longer or feel overwhelming, it’s a good idea to tell your therapist, who can adjust the pace with you. Serious side effects are uncommon when a therapist follows the full eight-phase process.

It has been revealed that the number of sessions you need depends on the memory you’re addressing and how long it has affected you. Some people feel relief after a few sessions, while longer-standing experiences often take more time. A common range is 6–12 sessions, but your timeline may be shorter or longer. Your therapist can give you a better sense of what to expect once they know your history.

It has been revealed that full EMDR needs a trained therapist, so it’s not something to try on your own. A therapist helps you reprocess memories and stay grounded if one feels overwhelming, which matters most with intense trauma.

Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, your phone buzzes.
  • Sources indicate that moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing.
  • Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your phone buzzes. It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago. You smile, then wonder why you smiled.

Sources indicate that moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing. For some people, staying connected feels natural because the habit, and maybe the care, is still there. For others, it makes healing feel harder. Every situation is different, and you’re allowed to take your time figuring out what works for you.

Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.

In a recent development, in some cases, you may be able to. Post-breakup friendships can be healthy and meaningful when the breakup was mutual, the relationship had little conflict, and both people have had time to grieve.

According to recent reports, that remarked, every friendship between exes is different. Researchers who study friendships after breakups describe two kinds. In one, both people have moved on and value the connection. In the other, one or both people stay in touch because of lingering attraction or reluctance to end things. The first kind can be rewarding. The second can make it harder to get over the breakup.

The dynamic you had with your ex matters, too. A study found that relationships shaped by high conflict, emotional dependency, or attachment anxiety may be harder to turn into a friendship afterward.

Before you decide anything, it may help to reflect on why you want to stay in touch. A few questions to sit with:.

What am I hoping this friendship gives me?

Am I trying to stay close to them or avoid the discomfort of letting go?

How would I feel if they started dating someone new?

If the last question stings, it may just mean that you need more time.

If you were the one who ended things, you might want friendship out of guilt or a wish to soften the loss. If you were the one who was left, you might view friendship as a potential path to getting back together.

If the answers don’t come right away, try a mindfulness practice. A few minutes of reflection or a short breathing exercise can help you sort through what you’re thinking and feeling.

💙 Try the Pause to Check In meditation on the Calm app.

If you’ve thought it through and still want to stay in touch, a few signs suggest a friendship may work. People who are securely attached often find it easier to stay friends after a breakup, but the list below can apply to anyone:.

You both see the breakup as mutual, with no ongoing hurt, resentment, or blame.

You’ve both accepted that the romantic relationship is over, with no unresolved romantic feelings.

There’s a reason for the friendship beyond comfort or familiarity, such as shared values, kids together, or a work connection.

In certain cases, staying friends can make healing harder or keep you from pouring energy into newly introduced parts of your life:.

You’re still in love with your ex and hoping the friendship leads somewhere.

The relationship involved emotional manipulation, control, or abuse.

The friendship gets in the way of latest relationships, like when a new partner feels uneasy about your connection.

You have different expectations for the friendship, which could leave one of you hurt.

💙 Discover the signs of having a toxic ex.

It has been revealed that it can be, especially since staying in touch can make it harder to let go. One study found that regular contact with an ex may slow emotional recovery. When you’re still part of each other’s routines, it can be harder to mourn the end of the relationship.

By contrast, a low-contact friendship, where you talk occasionally and keep to limits you’ve agreed on, is less likely to hold either of you back.

It has been revealed that how you feel after you talk is worth paying attention to. If you often feel sad, anxious, or unsettled, or you keep replaying the conversation, it may help to take some space.

💙 Read more on how to deal with a breakup when you’re hurting.

It may be appropriate to be friends with your ex, depending on your situation. It tends to work best when you’ve both moved on, the breakup didn’t involve harm, and the friendship fits both of your lives. If it also feels honest and comfortable to you, that’s a good sign.

Sources indicate that being friends with an ex isn’t automatically a red flag. If your partner is friends with an ex, how they handle it matters more than the friendship itself. A few questions to consider:.

Transparency: Do they talk about it openly, or does it feel secretive?

Priorities: Do they make time for you and the relationship?

Boundaries: Are there clear limits on the friendship, or does contact feel constant and undefined?

Responsiveness: When you raise a concern, does your partner listen or dismiss it?

In a recent development, if something doesn’t sit right, you could bring it up and see whether they listen, get defensive, or brush you off. If you’re the one staying friends with an ex, your newly introduced partner’s concerns are worth hearing out, even if nothing is wrong.

In a recent development, you don’t have to keep in touch with your ex after a breakup. Taking space is often healthy and necessary, and you can change your mind later. You can choose a full break, a time-limited break (“let’s not talk for a few months”), or a low-contact friendship.

Recent findings suggest that if you do stay in touch, some boundaries may protect your well-being. A few to consider:.

Recent findings suggest that set a pace. Daily texting can pull you back into old routines, so try starting with occasional check-ins instead.

Sources indicate that decide what’s off limits. That might mean dating lives, old conflicts, and late-night “remember when” talks.

Give yourself space online. Mute or unfollow for a while to adjust without ending the connection.

It has been revealed that plan a review and a way out. After a few months, ask whether the friendship still feels good. If it doesn’t, have a line ready, like “I think I need to take a step back for now.”.

Sources indicate that if you share children, a workplace, or a friend group, you may need to stay in touch. It’s often best to stick to logistics, like pickup times for the kids or project deadlines at work.

💙 Explore the Boundaries meditation on Calm.

There’s no set amount of time to wait before trying to be friends with an ex. Some people feel ready within months, while others take years. Some never feel ready or choose not to be friends, and that’s okay.

According to recent reports, A question to ask yourself is whether you can feel okay about the thought of your ex moving on. If that still hurts, you probably need more time.

It has been revealed that yes, being friends with an ex can sometimes turn into getting back together. Whether that’s a good thing depends on why your relationship ended and whether those reasons have changed.

Problems tied to circumstances, like bad timing or distance, may be easier to work through than core differences, like values, long-term goals, or how you communicate. If you get back together and those core differences haven’t changed, the same patterns can resurface.

It’s painful when one of you wants to stay friends after a breakup and the other doesn’t, and what helps depends on which side you’re on.

It has been revealed that if you’re the one being asked, you’re allowed to say “not yet” or “no.” If you’re unsure, you don’t have to answer right away. You might say:.

“I care about you, and I need some time before I know what this looks like.”.

“Can we revisit this in a few months?”.

“I’m not able to be friends right now, and I hope you can respect that.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re the one who wants friendship, the kindest move is to respect the space your ex has asked for. If you push for contact, it can get harder for you both to move on, even if giving them room hurts.

Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

The backpack hits the floor, and "How was your day?" gets a one-word answer: "Fine." Kids don’t always say what’s on their mind, but a little time and attention may help them open up.

In a recent development, world Children’s Day is a good moment for parents, caregivers, and teachers to ask kids how they’re feeling and listen without trying to fix anything. The day honors children’s rights, including the right to be heard.

Here’s a look at what the day is about, plus a few activities that can help kids feel understood, at home or in the classroom.

Sources indicate that world Children's Day is a global day of action for children, run by UNICEF. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 20. This year’s theme is “My day. My rights. My future.” It invites children to tell world leaders what kind of future they want.

According to recent reports, the day celebrates children and the rights they’re born with. In many places, children “take over” high-profile roles in media, sports, and government for the day. Landmarks light up blue to show support for children's rights.

Recent findings suggest that november 20 marks two milestones for children’s rights. On this date in 1959, the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child, a statement of shared ideals. Thirty years later to the day, it adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, a treaty that nations can commit to follow.

The Convention sets out the rights every child has, including the right to be safe, to play, and to have their opinions taken seriously. Nearly every country has formally agreed to follow it, and it’s the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history.

Industry observers note that countries around the world mark World Children’s Day. Many also celebrate a separate Children’s Day, most notably June 1, International Children's Day.

Sources indicate that some countries do pick dates of their own. Turkey celebrates on April 23, and India on November 14. The dates differ, but the idea is the same: it’s a day dedicated to the youngest members of a community.

You don’t need a substantial event to mark World Children’s Day. A meta-analysis on children and teens linked understanding emotions with better social skills and fewer behavior problems. Kids can build that understanding in everyday moments, like the ones below.

Industry observers note that kids may not know they have rights, but those who learn about them may feel more confident speaking up. UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention explains the rights in plain language.

Try: Read one or two rights together, then ask which feels most important to them.

Sources indicate that not every child has the words for how they feel. Invite them to sketch their day from morning to night, then have them walk you through it.

If they’re up for it, ask which part they loved most and which part felt hard. A drawing gives kids something concrete to point to as they talk, and that can feel easier than answering a broad question such as “How are you feeling?”.

Try: At home, pin the drawing to the fridge so your child can talk about it again if they’d like. In class, create an “Our Day” wall where kids can choose to share their drawings and spot the moments they had in common.

Recent findings suggest that when a child melts down, get curious about the feeling underneath. Help them put it into words: “It looks like you’re frustrated that it’s not your turn. Is that right?” Then listen carefully to their answer before you reassure them. “You’re fine” can sound dismissive, even when you mean well. When you talk about feelings this way, kids often learn to do it too.

Try: Post a chart of faces showing common feelings where kids can see it, and invite them to point to or say how they feel at the start of the day. Welcome any details they want to share.

💙 Once a major feeling has a name, here are coping skills for kids to try.

In a recent development, set aside a few minutes at dinner or morning circle time for everyone to share one high, one low, and one thing they’re thankful for. Take a turn yourself so kids feel more at ease sharing.

Just listen as kids share, and try not to talk them out of a hard feeling. Kids tend to manage feelings better when you respond with warmth instead of brushing them off.

Try: Pass around a talking object, such as a small stuffed animal. Whoever holds it has the floor, grown-ups included.

💙 On Calm, listen to Feel Thankful With Thomas, a four-minute meditation for little ones, or the Gratitude session from the Classroom Mindfulness Tools series.

According to recent reports, A few minutes of meditation can be a soothing way for kids to slow down and settle. Sessions can focus on anything from breathing and body awareness to gratitude and kindness, so there’s room to follow your child’s interests or needs. Kids can sit, lie down, or stand, and they can stop whenever they’d like.

Industry observers note that try: Belly breathing is a gentle place to start. Have your child lie down with a stuffed animal on their belly and watch it rise and fall as they breathe slowly.

It has been revealed that 💙 Explore Calm’s Mindfulness for Kids sessions for ages 3–4, ages 5–6, ages 7–10, and ages 11–13. For little ones, try the Calm Your Worries With Percy meditation from the Thomas & Friends Learn to Meditate series.

Reading together gives you some time to connect, and stories can spark conversations about feelings. Kids may find it easier to talk about how a character feels than how they do.

Pick a book where a character is going through difficult feelings, then pause and ask, “What do you think she’s feeling?”.

Try: At home, make the story the last part of your child’s bedtime routine to help them wind down. In class, read a few pages at the end of the day.

World Children's Day is on Friday, November 20, 2026. It falls on the same date every year.

Recent findings suggest that the UNICEF theme for World Children’s Day 2026 is "My day. My rights. My future." It encourages children to share their hopes for the future with world leaders.

The Convention on the Rights of the Child is the UN treaty behind the day. It names the rights every child has, including the right to be heard. For kids, it’s a written promise that their well-being and opinions count. Nearly every country has formally committed to it.

No, World Children’s Day and International Children’s Day are two separate observances with similar goals. World Children's Day is UNICEF's celebration on November 20, while International Children's Day is the June 1 observance held in many countries. Both honor children and their rights, so you can mark either one or both.

The best World Children’s Day activities for kids are often simple ones, such as inviting them to draw their day, holding a family or classroom check-in, or reading a story together. You can do these activities wherever makes sense, and even a few minutes counts.

You can start with UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention, and keep your explanation clear and specific. Try saying, “You have the right to feel safe, to play, and to say what you think.” Let them ask questions, and remind them that these rights belong to every child everywhere.
